The Great Sacrifice Rite:
The Glorious Secret Essence of Meditative Cultivation.
1. The venerable Guru is the power that constitutes the cause of all.
2. By that, the body consists of nine apertures.
Now, Bhāskararāya composes the ritual procedure for those meditations which have been taught for the sake of liberation by means of the *Bhāvanopaniṣad*.

Having restrained the vital breaths with the root mantra and performed the three nyāsas beginning with the ṛṣi-nyāsa, one should touch the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) while reciting: "Obeisance to the venerable Guru, who is the Self of the Suṣumṇā, consisting of the power of consciousness delimited by the faculty of discrimination."
Salutation to Prakāśānandanātha, whose self is the Sarasvatī of the right ear;
salutation to Vimarsānandanātha, whose self is the Śaṅkhinī of the left ear;
salutation to Anantānandanātha, whose self is Sarasvatī of the tongue.
Salutation to Śrī Jñānānandanātha, whose essence is Pūṣan in the form of the right eye;
salutation to Śrī Satyānandanātha, whose essence is Gāndhārī in the form of the left eye;
salutation to Śrī Pūrṇānandanātha, whose essence is Kuhū in the form of the banner.
Salutation to Svabhāvānandanātha, whose nature is the piṅgalā-form of the right nostril; salutation to Pratibhānandanātha, whose nature is the iḍā-form of the left nostril;
salutation to Sahajānandanātha, whose nature is the alambuṣā-form of the anus.
Thus, having touched those respective locations,
[one contemplates] the Śrīcakra in the form of the nine wheels.
4. Vārāhī, in the form of a father, is the mother of the offering deity Kurukullā.
5. The human goals are the oceans. 6. The body is the island of the nine gems.
7. It is endowed with the seven constituents, beginning with the skin, as well as hair.
His intentions are wish-fulfilling trees; his splendor is a garden of Kalpa trees.
Salutation to the body, which is the essence of the nine-fold Śrīcakra;
salutation to Vārāhī, who is the essence of the paternal components such as the bones and other parts;
salutation to Kurukullā, the deity of the *bali* offering, who is the essence of the maternal components such as the flesh and other parts.
*Namaḥ*.
Having thus performed the pervasion three times, [one offers salutation] to the Sugarcane Ocean, who is the nature of the dharma residing in the rear part of the body: *namaḥ* to the Sugarcane Ocean.
Salutation to the Ocean of Surā, whose nature is the form of the right side of the body;
salutation to the Ocean of Ghee, whose nature is the form of the eastern side of the body;
salutation to the Ocean of Milk, whose nature is the form of liberation on the northern side of the body.
Having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) three times with "Salutation to the island of the nine jewels for the self that is the body," [one should perform it] as follows: 1.

"Salutation to the island of the ruby (*puṣparāga*) for the self that is the flesh"; 2. "Salutation to the island of the sapphire (*nīla*) for the self that is the hair"; 3. "Salutation to the island of the lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*) for the self that is the skin."

Homage to the one whose essence is blood, the island of coral gems; homage to the one whose essence is semen, the island of pearl gems; homage to the one whose essence is marrow, the island of emerald gems.
Homage to the island of the vajra-jewel for the essence of bone; homage to the island of the gomedaka-jewel for the essence of fat; homage to the island of the ruby-jewel for the essence of vitality.
1. Homage to the presiding deity of flesh, the Sovereign of the Kālacakra.

2. Homage to the presiding deity of body hair, the Sovereign of the Rudracakra. 3. Homage to the presiding deity of skin, the Sovereign of the Mātṛcakra. 4. Homage to the presiding deity of blood, the Sovereign of the Ratnacakra.
Homage.
9. Being cultivated by the tongue, [the objects are] sweet, sour, bitter, pungent, and astringent.
The six seasons have the salty taste.
10. Knowledge is the offering of honor; the object of knowledge is the oblation; the knower is the priest.
The worship of the Śrīcakra consists in the contemplation of the non-difference between the knower, knowledge, and the object of knowledge.

5. Salutation to the presiding deity of semen, the Sovereign of the Ten Wheels. 6. Salutation to the presiding deity of marrow, the Sovereign of the Guru Wheel. 7. Salutation to the presiding deity of bone, the Sovereign of the Tattva Wheel. 8.
[Salutation to the presiding deity of marrow, the Sovereign of the Guru Wheel. (Note: Item 8 is a repetition of item 6 in the source text).
Salutation to the presiding deity of fat, the Mistress of the Graha-cakra (9). Salutation to the presiding deity of vitality, the Mistress of the Mūrti-cakra.
Salutation to the wish-fulfilling trees whose essence is volition. Salutation to the self of splendor.
Homage to Kalpakodyāna.
Homage to the spring season, whose essence is the sweet taste; homage to the summer season, whose essence is the sour taste.
Salutation to the rainy season, whose essence is the bitter taste; salutation to the autumn season, whose essence is the pungent taste;
salutation to the winter season, whose essence is the astringent taste; salutation to the cool season, whose essence is the salty taste.
Homage to the horses that are the nature of the sense faculties; homage to the elephants that are the nature of the objects of the sense faculties.
Salutation to the moat of water whose essence is compassion. Salutation to the ruby pavilion whose self is a mass of vital energy. Salutation to the special arghya whose self is knowledge.
Salutation to the oblation whose self is the object of knowledge. Salutation to the priest whose self is the knower.
Salutation to the Conscious Self, the illustrious Mahātripurasundarī.
Thus, having bowed with the mind preceded by the contemplation of each respective [deity],

and having rested for a moment through the contemplation that dissolves the names and forms of the knower, the knowledge, and the knowable, and by meditating upon their nature as pure consciousness alone. (Fifteen)
One should worship the eternal [goddesses], placing the hand upon the heart:
1. Tripurā, 2. Tripureśī, 3. Tripurasundarī, 4. Tripuravāsinī, 5. Tripurāśrīḥ, 6. Tripuramālinī, 7. Tripurāsiddhā, 8. Tripurāmbā, 9. [Tripurāmbikā].
In another tradition, Mahātripurasundarī is considered to be the nine sovereign goddesses of the wheels (cakreśvarī-navaka).
Salutation to Kāmeśvarī Nityā, who consists of one thousand four hundred and forty breaths, and whose form is the lunar day of the first (pratipad).
Salutation to the Nityā Bhagamālinī, who is the second lunar day (tithi) and whose nature consists of one thousand four hundred and forty-four breaths.
Salutation to the Nityaklinnā-nityā, who is the form of the third lunar day and whose nature consists of one thousand four hundred and forty breaths.
Salutation to the Nityā Bheruṇḍā, who is the fourth lunar day and whose nature consists of one thousand four hundred and forty breaths following that [previous count].
Salutation to the Nityā Vahnavāsinī, who is the fifth lunar day and whose nature consists of one thousand four hundred and forty breaths.
Salutation to the Nityā Mahāvajreśvarī, who is the form of the sixtieth lunar day, consisting of one thousand four hundred and forty breaths beyond that.
Salutation to Śivadūtī Nityā, who is the seventh lunar day, consisting of one thousand four hundred and forty breaths.
Salutation to Tvaritā Nityā, who is of the form of the eighth lunar day and whose nature consists of one thousand four hundred and forty breaths following that.
Salutation to Kulasundarī Nityā, who is the ninth lunar day (tithi) consisting of one thousand four hundred and forty breaths following that.
Salutation to Nityānityā, who is the tenth lunar day, whose nature consists of one thousand four hundred and forty breaths.
Salutation to Nīlapatākānityā, who is the eleventh lunar day (tithi) consisting of one thousand four hundred and forty breaths.

11. Necessity (niyati), the aesthetic sentiments such as the erotic (śṛṅgāra) and others, the supernatural powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and others, and [the qualities] consisting of desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, envy, merit, and demerit, beginning with the Brahmī [powers].
The eight powers; 12. the ninefold foundation, the powers of the mudrās.
Salutation to the eternal goddess Vijayānityā, who is the twelfth lunar day (tithi) and whose nature consists of one thousand four hundred and forty-four breaths;
salutation to her whose nature consists of one thousand four hundred and forty-four breaths following that.
Salutation to the eternal goddess Sarvamaṅgalā, who is the form of the thirteenth lunar day (trayodaśī-tithi);
salutation to the eternal goddess Jvālāmālinī, who is the form of the fourteenth lunar day (caturdaśī-tithi) and whose essence consists of one thousand four hundred and forty breaths (śvāsa).
Salutation to the Nityā Citrā, who is the full-moon lunar day and whose nature consists of one thousand four hundred and forty breaths following that;
some also recite the mantras of the respective Nityās at the beginning of each [section]; this is the meditation on the Nityās.

Or rather, it should be performed at the very end. Having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) in the locations to be mentioned later with the mantra, "Obeisance to the line of the first square" (*caturaśrādyarekhāyai namaḥ*).
Salutation to the self whose nature is the peaceful rasa (*śānta-rasa*) in the form of the right buttock, for the attainment of the power of minuteness (*aṇimā-siddhi*).
Salutation to the self whose nature is the marvelous rasa (*adbhuta-rasa*) in the form of the tips of the fingers of the right hand, for the attainment of the power of lightness (*laghimā-siddhi*).

Salutation to the one whose form is the right hip, whose nature is the aesthetic flavor of compassion (karuṇa-rasa), for the attainment of greatness (mahimā-siddhi). Salutation to the one whose form is the tips of the toes of the right foot, whose nature is the aesthetic flavor of heroism (vīra-rasa), for the attainment of lordship (īśitva-siddhi). Salutation to the one whose form is the tips of the toes of the left foot, whose nature is the aesthetic flavor of humor (hāsya-rasa), for the attainment of power over others (vaśitva-siddhi).

Salutation to the form of the left hip, whose nature is the loathsome sentiment (*bībhatsa-rasa*), for the attainment of the power of irresistible will (*prākāmya-siddhi*). Salutation to the form of the tips of the fingers of the left hand, whose nature is the furious sentiment (*raudra-rasa*), for the attainment of the power of enjoyment (*bhukti-siddhi*).
Salutation to the form of the left shoulder and back, whose nature is the terrifying sentiment (*bhayānaka-rasa*), for the attainment of the power of desire (*icchā-siddhi*).
Salutation to the form of the root of the crest, whose nature is the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa), for the attainment of the power of acquisition (prāpti-siddhi).
Salutation to the form of the back of the crest, whose nature is necessity (niyati), for the attainment of all desires (sarvakāma-siddhi).

Having performed the pervasive placement (nyāsa) within that [square] with the mantra "Obeisance to the central line of the square," [one places]:
"Obeisance to Brāhmī, whose nature is Desire, in the form of the two big toes";
"Obeisance to Māheśvarī, whose nature is Wrath, in the form of the right side."
Salutation to Kaumārī, whose form is the head and whose nature is greed;
salutation to Vaiṣṇavī, whose form is the left side and whose nature is delusion; salutation to Vārāhī, whose form is the left knee and whose nature is pride.
Salutation to Indrāṇī, whose nature is envy, in the form of the right knee;
salutation to Cāmuṇḍā, whose nature is merit, in the form of the right upper arm;
salutation to Mahālakṣmī, whose nature is sin, in the form of the left upper arm.

Having performed the pervasive placement (nyāsa) with "Obeisance to the final line of the square," one should then perform the placement for the thousand-petaled lotus at the base, which has the form of the two big toes,
with "Obeisance to the Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī Mudrā."
Salutation to the power of the Sarvavidrāviṇī mudrā, whose form is on the right side and whose essence is the Mūlādhāra;
salutation to the power of the Sarvākarṣiṇī mudrā, whose form is at the head and whose essence is the Svādhiṣṭhāna.
Salutation to the one whose form is on the left side, the essence of the Maṇipūra [cakra]; salutation to the Śakti of the Sarvavaśaṅkarī Mudrā.
Salutation to the self of the Unstruck (Anāhata) at the left knee, to the power of the Sarvonmādinī mudrā;
salutation to the self of the Pure (Viśuddhi) at the right knee, to the power of the Sarvamahāṅkuśā mudrā.
Salutation to the Self in the form of the right thigh, the source of Indra, who is the power (*śakti*) of all *khecarī-mudrās*.

Salutation to the Self in the form of the left thigh, the source of Aja, who is the power of all *bīja-mudrās*. Salutation to the Self in the form of the thousand-petaled lotus above the *dvādaśānta*, which is the source of all *yoni-mudrās*.
Salutation to Mudrā,
whose essence consists of the nine supports in the form of the big toes; salutation to the all-pervading three-sectioned Mudrā.

Having touched those respective locations with the mantra "Salutation to Tripurā, the Sovereign of the Heart-form Trailokyamohana-cakra," and having contemplated all these [deities] as non-different from one's own self,
one should contemplate the unlimited nature of the Self.
Salutation to one's own self in the form of the manifest Yoginī, for the sake of attaining the siddhi of aṇimā.
13. Earth, water, fire, air, space, the ear, the skin, the eye, the tongue, the nose, speech, the feet, the hands, the anus, the generative organ, and the modification of the mind.
The sixteen powers, beginning with Kāmākarṣiṇī.

Or, one should meditate preceded by the ritual application: "Salutation to Aparicchinnasvātmātman, the mudrā that agitates all. Then, having performed the pervasive placement (nyāsa) with "Salutation to the sixteen-petaled lotus," [one places it] on the back of the right ear as the essence of earth.
Salutation to the eternal digit Kāmākarṣiṇī, whose nature is the right shoulder; salutation to the eternal digit Budhyākarṣiṇī, whose nature is the self consisting of intellect;
salutation to the eternal digit Ahaṃkārākarṣiṇī, whose nature is the light consisting of the right elbow.
Salutation to the eternal digit Śabdākarṣiṇī Nityā, whose nature is the wind residing in the back of the right hand.

Salutation to the eternal digit (Nityākalā) Rūpākarṣiṇī, whose essence is the space of the right thigh and who attracts touch; salutation to the eternal digit (Nityākalā) Rasākarṣiṇī, whose essence is the skin of the right ankle and who attracts form; salutation to the eternal digit (Nityākalā) Gandhākarṣiṇī, whose essence is the sense of hearing of the right knee and who attracts taste.
Salutation to the eternal digit (nityākalā) Gandhākarṣiṇī, whose nature is the right sole of the foot and whose essence is the sense of smell;
salutation to the eternal digit Cittākarṣiṇī, whose nature is the left sole of the foot and whose essence is the sense of taste.

Salutation to the eternal digit Smṛtyākarṣiṇī Nityā, whose form is the left ankle and whose essence is speech. Salutation to the eternal digit Dhairyākarṣiṇī Nityā, whose form is the left knee and whose essence is the sense of smell.

Salutation to the eternal digit Nāmākarṣiṇī, whose essence is the form of the left thigh and the hands; salutation to the eternal digit Bījākarṣiṇī, whose essence is the form of the back of the left hand and the feet.
Salutation to the eternal digit Ātmākarṣiṇī Nityākalā, whose nature is the anus in the form of the left elbow;
salutation to the eternal digit Amṛtākarṣiṇī Nityākalā, whose nature is the generative organ in the form of the left shoulder.
Salutation to the eternal digit (Nityākalā), who is the self whose mind is transformed by the form [seen] behind the left ear and who draws the body [toward herself];
salutation to Tripureśvarī, the sovereign of the wheel that fulfills all desires in the form of the heart.
14. The eight [faculties] beginning with Anaṅgakusuma are the cognitions termed speech, grasping, movement, excretion, pleasure, rejection, acquisition, and equanimity.

Alambuṣā, Kuhū, Viśvodarā, Vāruṇī, Hastijihvā, Yaśovatī, Payasvinī, Gāndhārī, Pūṣā, Śaṅkhinī, Sarasvatī, Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Suṣumnā— these fourteen channels (nāḍīs) correspond to the fourteen powers (śaktis), beginning with Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī.
Salutation to the self-nature of the form of Guptayoginī, for the attainment of the supernatural power of levitation (laghimā).
"Salutation to the Mudrā who dissolves all, whose own self is of an unenclosed form;
salutation to the eight-petaled lotus"—having thus performed the pervasive placement (nyāsa) within that, [one should recite]:
"Salutation to Anaṅgakusumā, whose nature is speech in the form of the right conch."
Salutation to Anaṅgamekhalā, whose nature is the appropriation of the form of the right clavicle;
salutation to Anaṅgamadanā, whose nature is the movement toward the form of the right thigh;
salutation to Anaṅgamadanāturā, whose nature is the emission of the form of the right ankle.
Salutation to Anaṅgarekhā, whose nature is the bliss of the form of the left elbow;

salutation to Anaṅgavegā, whose nature is the intellect called the relinquishment of the form of the left thigh; salutation to Anaṅgāṅkuśā, whose nature is the intellect called the material cause of the form of the left collarbone.
Salutation!
Salutation to Anaṅgamālinī, whose nature is the intellect known as equanimity (upekṣā) and who has the form of the left peak (vāmaśikhara).
Salutation to Tripurasundarī, the sovereign of the heart-center wheel (hṛdayopasarvasaṃkṣobhaṇacakra).
"Salutation to my own self in the form of the most secret Yoginī, for the attainment of greatness;
salutation to my own self in the form of the unlimited, to the Sarvākarṣiṇī Mudrā;
salutation to the fourteen-spoked wheel"—having thus performed the pervasive placement (nyāsa) within that.
Salutation to the power Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī, whose essence is the Ālaṃbuṣā channel, located in the central region of the forehead.

16. To the ten vital winds—prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, samāna, nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya—who are the outer ten-spoked deities beginning with the bestowers of all siddhis; and to the Śakti who subdues all, whose nature is the cave on the right side of the forehead: salutation!
Salutation to the power Sarvākarṣiṇī, whose form is the right cheek and whose self is the belly of the universe.
Salutation to the Self in the form of Varuṇī on the right shoulder, who is the power that gladdens all.
Salutation to the power Sarvasaṃmohinī, whose nature is the elephant’s tongue (hastijihvā) located in the form of the right side;
salutation to the power Sarvastambhinī, whose nature is Yaśovatī located in the form of the right thigh.
Salutation to the Self in the form of the milk-river of Dakṣa’s shanks, the power that causes all to yawn.
Salutation to the power (śakti) named Sarvavaśaṃkarī, whose essence is Gāndhārī, residing in the left calf and thigh.
Salutation to the Śakti Sarvarañjinī, whose essence is the beautiful Pūṣan of the left thigh.
Salutation to the self in the form of Śaṅkhinī on the left side, the power Sarvonmādinī; salutation to the self in the form of Sarasvatī on the left shoulder, the power Sarvārthasādhinī.
Salutation to the Śakti named Sarvasaṃpattipūraṇī, whose form resides in the left cheek.
Salutation to the Power consisting of all mantras, whose nature is Piṅgalā on the left side of the forehead.
Salutation to the Śakti, whose nature is the Suṣumṇā situated at the back of the forehead, who brings about the destruction of all dualities.
Salutation to Tripuravāsinī, the Sovereign of the Wheel who bestows all auspiciousness in the form of the heart;
salutation to the self-nature of one's own soul in the form of the Sampradāya Yoginī, for the attainment of the power of lordship (īśitva-siddhi).
Salutation to the Mudrā who brings all things under her control, whose own self is of an undivided form.

Having performed the pervasive placement (vyāpaka-nyāsa) with "Obeisance to the outer ten-spoked wheel," [one places] "Obeisance to the Goddess who bestows all accomplishments, whose essence is the vital breath in the form of the right eye."
Salutations to the Goddess who bestows all prosperity, whose form is the downward breath at the root of the nose.

17. Due to the differentiation of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) through contact with this wind, it becomes fivefold by way of its primary functions as *prāṇa*: namely, the expeller (*recaka*), the digester (*pācaka*), the dryer (*śoṣaka*), the burner (*dāhaka*), and the moistener (*plāvaka*).
The digestive fire (jaṭharāgni) is fivefold according to the predominance of the [five] nāgas: Kṣāraka, Udgāraka, Kṣobhaka, Jṛmbhaka, and Mohaka; these reside within the bodies of human beings.
They digest the fivefold food consisting of what is chewed, eaten, sucked, licked, and drunk.
These ten fire-powers (vahnikalās), beginning with Sarvajñā and residing within the inner decagon,
are salutations to the goddess Sarvapriyaṅkarī, who is the nature of the vyāna breath and the form of the left eye.

Salutation to the Goddess who bestows all auspiciousness, whose nature is the fire in the right corner of the abdomen; salutation to the Goddess who grants all desires, whose nature is the air in the left corner of the abdomen; salutation to the Goddess who liberates from all suffering, whose nature is the serpent in the left knee.
Salutations to the Goddess, who is of the nature of the horse-headed Kūrma and who pacifies all death.
Salutation to the Goddess Sarvavighnavināśinī, whose nature is the right knee and the southeast corner; salutation to the Goddess Sarvāṅgasundarī, whose nature is the belly and the southwest corner.
Salutation to the Goddess who bestows all auspicious fortune, whose essence is the form of the conqueror of wealth (Dhananjaya) located in the corner of the belly.
Salutation to Tripurāśrī, the Sovereign of the Heart-form All-Accomplishing Wheel.
Salutation to one's own self in the form of the Kulakaula Yoginīs, for the sake of attaining mastery.
Salutation to the Seal of Universal Intoxication, whose own self is undivided from the Self.
Having performed the pervasive placement (nyāsa) within that [space] with the mantra "Salutation to the internal ten-spoked wheel" (antardaśāracakra), [one should proceed].
Salutation to Sarvajñādevī, whose nature is the fire of exhalation (*recaka*) from the right nostril.
Salutation to the Goddess of All Powers, whose essence is the fire of digestion, the form of which is the palate of Dakṣa.
20. Cold, heat, pleasure, pain, desire, goodness (*sattva*), passion (*rajas*), and darkness (*tamas*)— these and others are the eight powers (*śakti*).
Salutation to the Goddess who bestows all sovereignty, whose nature is the fire that consumes the form of the right breast;
salutation to the Goddess who consists of all-knowledge, whose nature is the fire that burns the form of the right testicle.
Salutation to the Goddess who destroys all diseases, whose nature is fire that dries up the form of the skin.
Salutation to the Goddess whose nature is the support of all, who is the essence of the left testicle, the form of the earth, salt, fire, and the self.

Salutation to the Goddess Sarvapāpaharā, whose nature is fire and who manifests as the form of the left breast; salutation to the Goddess Sarvānandamayī, whose nature is fire and who agitates the form of the left cheek.
Salutation to the Goddess whose nature is all-protection, who is the self of the dwarf, the nose, the yawning one, and fire.
Salutation to the Goddess who bestows all desired fruits, whose nature is the fire that deludes forms at the tip of the nose.
Salutation to Tripuramālinī, the sovereign of the wheel that provides all protection in the form of the heart.
Salutation to one's own self in the form of the Yoginī of the Inner Essence, for the attainment of the power of irresistible will.

Having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) within that [space] with the words "Salutation to the Self whose own nature is of an undivided form; salutation to the Great Goad-Seal (*sarvamahāṅkuśamudrā*);
salutation to the eight-cornered wheel," one should then [place]:
"Salutation to the Goddess of Speech (*vāgdevatā*), Vaśinī, who is the cool-natured aspect of the right side of the chin."
Salutation to Kāmeśvarī, the goddess of speech, whose nature is heat and who resides on the right side of the throat.
Salutation to Modinī, the goddess of speech, whose nature is the bliss of the form on the right side of the heart.

Salutation to the goddess Vimalā-vāgdevatā, whose nature is the form of the right side of the navel and who is the self of suffering; salutation to the goddess Aruṇā-vāgdevatā, whose nature is the form of the left side of the navel and who is the self of desire.
Salutation to the victorious goddess of speech, whose essence is the quality of goodness (sattva-guṇa) manifested as the left side of the heart.
Salutation to the goddess of speech Sarveśvarī, who is the nature of the quality of rajas in the form of the left side of the throat.
21. The five subtle elements (tanmātras), beginning with sound, are the five flower-arrows.
22. The mind is the sugarcane bow; 33. passion is the noose; 24. hatred is the goad;
25. the Unmanifest, Mahat, and Ego are the deities Kāmeśvarī, Vajreśvarī, and Bhagamālinī, who reside within the inner triangle.
Salutation to Kaulinī, the goddess of speech, whose essence is the quality of tamas in the form of the left side of the chin.
Salutation to Tripurāsiddhā, the Sovereign of the Wheel that removes all diseases in the form of the heart.
Salutation to the self-nature of the fire-form of the secret yoga, for the attainment of enjoyment.
Salutations to the one whose own self is of an undifferentiated form, the Sealed One of all sky-faring goddesses.
Salutation to the all-piercing arrows, which consist of the five subtle elements (tanmātras) in the form of the lower portion of the heart-triangle.

Now follows the recitation of the Peace Mantra (*śāntimantra*) of the Tripuropaniṣad, together with its commentary:
Oṃ! May my speech be established in my mind; may my mind be established in my speech.

My speech, engaged in the recitation of texts that expound the knowledge of reality, is always established in my mind; that is to say, the mind is the means by which the intended collection of words is communicated.

And my mind is established in speech: the collection of words that expounds the knowledge of the Self is intended by the mind for utterance. For speech and mind, when mutually supported, are able to comprehend a text concerning the meaning of knowledge in its entirety.

The sense is that in the absence of attentiveness of the mind, one might say something incoherent; likewise, in the absence of eloquence of speech, what is intended to be said is not articulated correctly. Therefore, a mutual compatibility between the two is prayed for.
Be manifest to me again and again.

Be the axle-pin of my Veda; what I have heard, do not let it slip away from me.

I shall speak the truth—meaning, may there never be a speaking of perverted meanings. "Truth" (ṛtam) is mental and "truthfulness" (satyam) is verbal; the meaning is that having reflected upon the reality of things with the mind, I shall speak it with my voice.
May that protect me; may it protect the speaker;
may it protect me, may it protect the speaker, may it protect the speaker. Om.
Peace, peace, peace.
May that reality of Brahman protect me, the disciple, through perfect awakening;

however, for the teacher, the fruit obtained through gaining such a disciple is the non-interruption of the tradition of knowledge (*vidyā-sampradāya*). By means of this recitation of the mantra:

First, the obstacles that hinder the acquisition of knowledge are removed; thereafter, however, the obstacles that give rise to doubt and contrary conceptions regarding the knowledge already attained are eliminated.
The repetition indicates the conclusion of the chapter. Thus ends the meaning of the peace-mantra (śāntimantra).

The three cities (pura) are also to be traversed; because she leads one to these three such cities, or because she is of their very nature, the Supreme Deity is called Tripurā. By worshipping her through the intellect as the Self, as a symbol (pratīka), with the motherly intellect, or even through ritual action, a mortal attains absolute liberation (kaivalya).

"She attains the state of *padam*," according to this statement from the *Śaktirahasya*, it is taught that even through the worship of the fivefold self, one attains the *Tripura* [state]. Therefore, she herself is the three cities (*tisraḥ puraḥ*), thus *Tripurā*; she is *Tripathā*, because she possesses three paths (*trayaḥ panthānaḥ*).

In the case of a *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in *pathin*, neuter gender does not apply simply because of the suffix *-ṇī*, due to the rule "of *pathin*, a numeral, and an indeclinable" (*pathasaṃkhyāvyayādeḥ*). The word *carṣaṇi* is found in the Vedic *Nighaṇṭu* as a synonym for progeny (*prajā*). That [city] in which all (*viśvāḥ*) people (*carṣaṇayaḥ*) reside is [described thus].
"Viśvacarṣaṇī" means the goddess who is the progenitor of all living beings.

Alternatively, this is what must be understood here: that very first intuition (*īkṣaṇa*) of Brahman, established by the Śruti in the passage, "It [Brahman] thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate,'" is itself the progenitor of all, and it is of the nature of will (*icchā*) as well as the nature of action (*kṛti*). "It desired" (*sā aikṣata*).

From another scriptural passage, "They perform austerity," and from the scripture, "The power of knowledge and action is inherent," it is established that the primordial function— which is non-different from Brahman— is one alone,
consisting of the forms of knowledge, will, and action. That [function]...
Vṛtti itself is called "quiescent" because it consists of the collective totality of will, knowledge, and action.
She is called *Parā* because she is the subtle form that is the aggregate of the triad of Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī;
she is called *Ambikā* because she is the aggregate form of Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī. She...
The deity whose nature is peace is indeed the Bindu-cakra situated within the Śrīcakra. This has been stated in the Nityāhṛdaya, beginning with the exposition of the Supreme Brahman:
The Wheel of the Bindu (baindava-cakra) is that which has issued forth, is the locus of the waves of the universe, and consists of the three Mothers; and so forth.
And that very [city] is designated by the three qualifiers "tisraḥ puraḥ," "tripathā," and "viśvacarṣaṇī"; through these qualifiers,
expressed with both plural and singular numbers, [the nature of] the qualified object is indicated.
The state of having three forms and the state of being a single essence have been indicated.
Concerning Brahman as delimited by such a vision,
it is also stated in the Kālikā Purāṇa:
Her mandala is a triangle, and her earthly city (bhūpura) consists of three lines;
her mantra is said to have three syllables, and likewise she possesses a triple form.
The power of Kuṇḍalinī is threefold for the sake of the creation of the three deities.

"Because she is threefold in all three [states], she is therefore considered Tripurā. Having thus indicated her as the generator of the creation of meaning (*arthasṛṣṭi*), [the text] further indicates her as the generator of the creation of sound (*śabdasṛṣṭi*).

He explains where [this occurs]: "where" means in that Tripurā, whose forms are Śāntā, Ambikā, and so forth, wherein the "non-kas"—the sixteen letters beginning with 'a', the sixteen beginning with 'ka', and the sixteen beginning with 'tha'—are situated. The letters are situated there.

They exist perfectly and completely within the seed-syllable *vaṭa* (the banyan), just as a tree exists within its seed. Indeed, the letter *ha* is of the very nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), and thus it is not perceived separately in the form of an individual manifestation; for it is said: "The phoneme *ha*, which is a digit (*kalā*) and known as reflective awareness, is proclaimed [to be the supreme]. As for the letter *la*:

The letter *la* is not distinct from [the preceding letters]. The letter *kṣa*, however, is merely a combination of *ka* and *ṣa* and is not independent. Therefore, there are forty-eight *mātṛkās*. These alone are the *mātṛkās*. And so it is stated in the *Sūtasaṃhitā*:
"I bow to that supreme *kalā* which exists as one, as two, and likewise as sixteen, and which is divided into thirty-two varieties. Thus [it is said].

It is twofold through the division of vowels (*svara*) and consonants (*vyañjana*); the meaning is that the vowel has sixteen forms and the consonant has thirty-two divisions. In the two-word phrase beginning with "akṣara," the substitution of *jas* for *ṣaṣ* is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) usage. Thus, by the first half [of the verse].

Having taught the essential nature of the *bindu*-cakra, he speaks of the supreme goddess who presides over it and is to be worshipped, saying "presiding over": there is a certain deity who, having presided over this Tripurā— who has just been taught as being of the form of the *bindu*— exists.

According to the statement of Kātyāyana, "The verb *as* (to be), followed by *bhavantī* [the present participle], exists even when not explicitly employed in the first person," there is an ellipsis of the verb *as*. Alternatively, it may be construed with the action expressed by the verb in the subsequent mantra. That deity is ageless (*ajara*), meaning free from death.
In the context of the root *jṛ* meaning "decay of age," the term "decay of age" (*vayohāni*) refers specifically to the destruction of youth.
"Ancient" (*purāṇī*) means beginningless. Among the most renowned deities—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others—she is the greatest, being devoid of birth.

She is the most excellent; she is of the same nature as the majesty of those deities. The meaning is that this [Goddess] alone is the source of the greatness even of other deities, for it is through meditation upon her alone that they attain their majesty.
Since numerous instances are shown in the Tripuropaniṣad and in the Purāṇas, Tantras, and other texts following it, of Vidyās worshipped by Śiva, Viṣṇu, and others, [it is said]:
"Śambhu worships the auspicious Goddess, who consists of the power of mantra."

This is because the various types of images worthy of worship by all the gods are described in detail in the *Padma Purāṇa*. Furthermore, it is according to the maxim: "A beggar ought not to beg from another beggar when there is another who is not a beggar."
The implied meaning, however, is that the worship of the Supreme Deity alone is superior to the worship of other deities;
this very point was stated by us in the *Paraśivastava*.
Since you possess the sovereignty granted by you, how could you beg from other lords of the gods— those mendicants headed by Śakra, Brahmā, and Hari— for the sake of another Supreme Śiva?
I am a mendicant; though ignorant, I am also the *ukthya* sacrifice, which is a constituent part of a hundred variations of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāhakra-tu*).
It desires the characteristics of the *jyotiṣṭoma* and *ukthya*, but not the characteristics of the *dvādaśāha* *ukthya*.
By means of the Brahmanic signs such as "the immovable" (*ajera*), the deity presiding over the *bindu-cakra* [is indicated].

It is thus stated that [the object] is indeed the Supreme Brahman. The feminine gender is used with the intention of making the word "Devatā" the substantive; for this very reason, there is a neuter designation in another Śruti. And so it is clearly stated by the Atharvaṇas:
They declare:
"The city of Ayodhyā of the gods has eight wheels and nine gates; within it is a golden treasure-chest."

The heavenly world is enveloped in light; within that golden, triangular sheath, it is established in a triple support. Whatever therein possesses self-consciousness, that indeed the knowers of Brahman know.

Above the eight wheels beginning with the *bhūpura* and ending with the triangle, there is a sheath (*kośa*), which is to say the *bindu* that contains within it the three forms. Within that is a great being (*mahadbhūta*) called a *yakṣa*. It is designated by the term "yakṣa" because it is unfit for external worship.
Only those who know Brahman know that within their own self; no others do. This is the meaning; such is the detailed explanation in the *Setubandha*.
Having thus described the *binducakra*,

the author speaks the second verse, beginning with "navayonīḥ," in order to teach the wheel consisting of nine wombs (*navayoni*), which is the unified form of the triangle, the eight-cornered [figure], and the two curves.
They assumed nine wombs, nine wheels, nine yogas, and nine yoginīs.
She is the sovereign lady over the wheel of the nine, the auspicious one, possessing the nine mudrās and the ninefold auspiciousness of the earths.
They have established three cities with nine wombs; though it is a single *bindu*-wheel, it assumes a triple form in each instance because it possesses a threefold nature.
This is a form derived from the Vedic root *dīdhīṅ*, meaning "to shine" or "to play. And its illumination is as follows:
In this context, the intended meaning is that manifestation itself is, in effect, production.

Within the limitation of Śāntā, he brought forth the three deities— will-power (icchā-śakti), action-power (kriyā-śakti), and knowledge-power (jñāna-śakti); and within the limitation of Ambikā, he generated Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra in female forms, named the powers Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī.

The meaning is that the goddesses of speech—Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī—generated [the mantra] by means of the limitation of the supreme state (*paratva*). Alternatively, the syntactical connection is: "That very Supreme Deity, presiding over this Tripurā, created the nine *yoni*s. These [nine *yoni*s] are indeed the nine deities themselves.

The path of latent impressions (*vāsanādhvan*) consists in their being transformed into the nature of the wheel of nine wombs (*navayonicakra*). Furthermore, the nine wheels beginning with the *Trailokyamohana*—whether already arisen or yet to arise—exist within those very nine wombs in the form of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). This is what he expresses by saying "the nine wheels."

"They assumed nine wombs as creators" means that the nine-womb wheel (*navayonicakra*) is produced by two triangular power-shapes (*śaktitrikoṇa*) and one fire-triangle (*vahnitrikoṇa*). Since there are three lines for each triangle, the conjunctions of these nine lines likewise result in nine forms of triangles. Thus, they assumed the nine Yoginīs.

The sense is that because the nine wheels exist here, the group of nine Yoginīs—Prakaṭā and the rest—located therein also resides right here within the nature of the corners. This is because of such conventional usage as: "That supreme light above is unconditioned by space and time," and so forth.

It is understood that the manifold expansion beginning with the *bindu*-cakra, delimited by space and other factors, exists below and beneath Brahman. It is precisely based on this that the "Meru-expansion" (*meruprastāra*) of the Śrīcakra is established. Therefore, within a single cakra, there is everything from the outer enclosure (*bhūpura*) up to the *bindu*.

Above and above are the nine levels; their presiding deities are also named Tripurā, Cakreśvarī, and so forth, or they are not [distinct]. He says that they too abide within the nine wombs (navayoni) in a subtle form: "in the wheel of the nine."

"Even the sovereigns of the earth have established the nine wombs as their agents. The term "Syonā" (the Auspicious) is an epithet of Cakreśvarī; the meaning is that she is the cause of happiness. The nine mudrās, beginning with Saṃkṣobhiṇī and ending with Yoni, are also situated right here. However, the Nine Auspicious Ones (Navabhadra) are [described] in the Tantra.

"Dharma and adharma are disclosed, as well as the selves, the means of knowledge (mātṛ), the objects of knowledge (meya), and likewise the light. This refers to the group of nine: merit (puṇya), demerit (pāpa), the self (ātmā), the inner self (antarātmā), the supreme self (paramātmā), the self of knowledge (jñānātmā), the knower (pramātā), the object of knowledge (prameya), and valid cognition (pramā).
The exposition of the nature of the fourfold self should be seen in the *Ātmopaniṣad*.

"This wheel consists of nine aspects, with its mantras divided ninefold"—from such an expansion [of the text] we learn this. Alternatively, the mantras may be understood by means of the term *bhadrāpada*.
Regarding these, some say they are the mantras of the Nine Mistress of the Wheel (*cakreśvarī*), while others maintain, on account of their proximity, that they are indeed the mudrā-mantras.

But this is logical. The condensed meaning is that within the *saṃhāracakra* itself—which consists of the three wheels in the form of the Bindu, the Triangle, and the Octagon—the entire *śrīcakra* exists in a subtle form. This applies to the methods of abbreviated worship for times of distress (*āpatkāla*).
The procedure for the worship of the deities, beginning with Vasu and Koṇa and ending with Bindu, which is found in the Tantras— of that,
this very [Vedic] scripture is the root authority. In all these instances,
the corroborative statements from the Tantras and Purāṇas are not written here for fear of prolixity.
Now, in order to teach the wheel of maintenance (*sthiticakra*), which consists of two tens and two *anvaśras*, he recites the third verse:
(3) "She was one; she was nine; she was nineteen; she was twenty-nine."
May the forty-three kindling-sticks enter [the fire] like longing mothers.
From these nine sources, it is said, "He sat alone," the tenfold group of elements arose—namely, the five subtle elements and the five gross elements.
From those, through the distinction of gross and subtle, the tenfold group of objects beginning with sound and the limbs of the body arose; and from those...

The five organs of action, the five organs of knowledge, and the four internal organs—thus the fourteen were born. All these deities, being female in form, are indeed of the nature of the womb (*yoni*). All this [is as follows]:
"The group of ten consisting of the elements and the subtle essences (*tanmātra*), by virtue of being the objective support for manifestation,

has its form as the throbbing sixteen-spoked [wheel] explained in the Tantra" and so forth. That very same process is here taught, preceded by a restatement of what was previously mentioned, beginning with the word "the first."
In the beginning, she alone existed as the cause of the entire world, in the form of the *bindu-cakra*. Then she became ninefold through the nature of the nine *yoni*s.
Then she became nineteenfold, consisting of the nineteen *svarūpa*s; that is, the nine *yoni*s and the internal ten-spoked *yoni*s.

The word "twenty" (*viṃśat*) and so forth is Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). Then, by the union of the twenty-nine [petals] with the outer ten-petaled [lotus], there are thirty-nine. Then, by the union of the forty-three—the three [inner petals] and the fourteen [outer ones]—there is a single form consisting of forty-three petals.

The meaning is that the Goddess has been born. Because the *bindu*-cakra has the form of an interior space (*antarākāra*), it is not enumerated among the "single-seated" (*ekāsana*) forms shaped like a womb (*yoni*). Blazing brightly, kindled by fuel, may these [energies] enter me this morning; may they penetrate me.
This is the prayer of the author of the hymn, based on the fact that even his own body has the form of the Śrīcakra.

The meaning is: "Just as cows, though in reality free from desire, enter quickly from the forest to the cow-pen out of longing for their calves—as if they were desiring them—so too may these [waters] enter. This is the very Vedic text.
The root of the procedures for the placement of the wheels (*cakranyāsa*) found in the tantras is this:
because these very deities are to be placed within one's own body, [one should recite], "May all those Yoginīs make my body their abode."
The root of that [realization] also arises from the correspondence between the deposition of power (śaktinyāsa), the mantra, and the liṅga.
Now, in order to teach the two lotuses distinguished by three circles that remain in the *sṛṣṭicakra*, he recites the fourth verse, beginning with "ūrdhvajvalat" (p.
4) That light of the upward-flaming fire is not darkness, nor is it horizontal; it is undecaying and free from dust.
It is the delighting and gladdening light of the moon; these indeed adorn the circles of the mandala.

In the downward-facing lotus, there exist two [circles] consisting of fourteen spokes, eight petals, and sixteen petals respectively. Likewise, above, there is only one outer circle surrounding the pericarp; thus, according to the doctrine of some, there are three circles. For this very reason, it has the form of the *jyeṣṭhā* [vowels].
Regarding the phrase "three circles" (*bhramitraya*) in the passage "four-cornered, having the form of Vāmā,
with three circles," the term *bhramitraya* indicates two lotuses situated within the two spaces between the three circles.

The interpretation of the ancient teachers is appropriate. Even regarding the statement, "O Dear One, the two lotuses joined with three circles are of the nature of Agni and Soma according to the Śāktas," this very same interpretation applies. And those circles consist of the three qualities (guṇas) of Agni, Soma, and Sūrya.

By the description of the verse concerning the *prakṛti*, it should be understood that the two lotuses situated between them have also been described. As for the literal meaning [of the subsequent verses], it concerns the wheels of persistence (*sthiticakra*) and the upper wheels: first, *tamaḥ* (darkness), which consists essentially of the determined quality of *tamas*, is named "Blazing" (*jvalana*).
It became a circle of light;
by the qualification "blazing upwards," the nature of the flame as being like fire is confirmed.

Furthermore, by the observation of collyrium in the upper portion, there is a reinforcement of its nature as darkness; for this very reason, the indeclinable *vai* is used to dispel any suspicion of inconsistency in describing that which consists of light as being of the nature of darkness. Beyond that is the horizontal circle of light, which extends transversely.

Because it was red, it became the quality of *rajas*. And that took the form of the sun, since the upward and horizontal extension of fire and the sun is directly perceptible. As the learned have said:
"It moves transversely for the one whose charioteer is the thighless [wind], and its upward flaming is well known for the consumer of oblations.
Thus, the qualifier "undecaying" (ajara) is intended to strengthen the distinction from fire. Therefore...

*Modanaṃ* means that which produces pleasure derived from sense objects. From the moon, a circle of light (*jyotirmaṇḍala*) arose. By the word "bliss" (*ānanda*), its nature as consisting of the quality of *sattva* is expressed, because it is precisely that which is predominant in *sattva* that manifests the bliss of Brahman. *U. vai. u.* is used for gentle address. *Vai* [is a particle of emphasis].
Or, it has the sense of the particle *eva* (only/indeed). Thus, three circles are drawn. These adorn the Mothers, making them beautiful.
The Śrīcakra is distinguished by pairs of lotuses situated within the intervals between the three circles.

The meaning is that it is not merely capable of performing the ritual action, but is also free from mental exhaustion; the intention is that worship beginning with *mantra* and ending with *bindu* is intended for times of emergency (*āpad-kālika*).
To teach the ninth wheel, which consists of an underground chamber,
he speaks the fifth verse beginning with "tisraścarekhā" (three lines).

And the three lines are the abodes of the earth—the triple heavens, consisting of the three qualities and the three lights. This city is the fulfiller of all that fulfills; herein Madana sports with Madanī.

In other tantras, three circles are seen to be prescribed outside the two lotuses, in addition to the two circles of the pericarp (*karṇikā*). According to that view, the phrase "and three lines" should be understood as referring only to these three circular lines; it is not [to be understood otherwise].
And this being so, it should not be argued that there is an inconsistency in describing three mandalas as remaining solely from the pericarp (karṇikā), because in the *Tantrarāja*,
outside the sixteen-syllable [mantra], there is a circular boundary-line distinct from the eight-petaled circle.

For it is logical that this Śruti [text] is rooted in that [tradition], as established by its exposition. The grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of "the earth," "the dwellings," and "the three lines" is an unstrained meaning. They themselves are the "three heavens" (*triviṣṭapa*), consisting of the three worlds, because they are the abode of the deities.

Or they have the form of heaven. They possess the three qualities (*triguṇa*), meaning they consist of the three *guṇas*; they are the "threefold illuminations" (*triprakāśa*), meaning they consist of the illumination of the three circles in the form of the sun, moon, and fire.

He concludes the description of the Śrīcakra with the words "etad" (this). Described in four and a half [verses], this city is like the City of Śrī—a wheel (*cakra*) that is the dwelling place of the Supreme Deity along with her retinue. It is for those who fulfill, meaning it fulfills the heart's desires of the devotees.

It fulfills even Śiva, Viṣṇu, and the others; it fulfills all desires. Here, in this Śrīcakra, Madana is renowned as Śivakāmeśvara, and Madanī as Śivakāmasundarī, through the expansion of various forms such as the *aṇimā* [powers] which are their own rays of light.
The meaning is "sporting. Alternatively, there is a word division as *madanī ā*, where the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to the rule for [denoting] a woman associated with a man.

The construction is "they spread out" (*āprathete*), because of the grammatical rule permitting [the use of the suffix] even when [the verb] follows [another word] in Vedic usage, and also when [words] are separated [by others]. All those divine forms which are found in various fields under different names in the Purāṇas and the Tantras belong to her.
In order to teach "it is thus," he recites the sixth verse.
(6) She is Madantikā, the proud one, auspicious and fortunate; she is Sundarī, endowed with purity, modesty, contentment, and beloved; she is Puṣṭā, Lakṣmī, Umā, Lalitā, and she who speaks sweetly.
Regarding the phrase "Madantikā": in the *Padmapurāṇa*, during the enumeration of the Devī-tīrthas, several forms are mentioned, such as Lalitādevī at Prayāga, and so forth;
likewise, she is named Maṅgalā in Laṅkā and Bhadrasundarī on Trikūṭa.
Mahālakṣmī resides in the Karavīra tree, and Rumādevī resides in Vināyaka.

"Nourishment in the Devadāru forest, intelligence in the Kaśmīra region, and likewise contentment in the land of the Lord of Vatsa"— these and other such forms [of his] are to be sought in their respective places.

The fourteen verses beginning with "madantike" are an illustration of Viśālākṣī and others in Vārāṇasī; the meaning is that whatever form of the Goddess it may be, she is indeed the same one even while she is thus lamenting. [This refers to] the word *lālapanti*.

"Another [type of word] is that which, while uttering a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), expresses a case-ending (*vibhakti*) as a qualifier for the meaning of that nominal stem"— this is stated because such usage is observed in the *Śābarabhāṣya*. Alternatively, [it refers to] fifteen syllables.
These are the fifteen deities. Regarding the term "śuddhimattā," the Atharvaṇa recension reads "siddhimattā."
In order to prescribe the worship of the deity thus described,
he utters the seventh verse, beginning with "imā vijñāya" (having known these).

(7) Having realized this, they rejoice with the nectar of immortality, satiating their own seat with the flowing stream [of bliss]. Dwellers upon the back of the great celestial vault, they enter the supreme abode of the Triple City.

Having understood this aforementioned supreme deity— having known it through its various specific distinctions and having undertaken its worship by means of approaching a guru, initiation, and so forth— having accepted it, [one should meditate].

Their own seat (*svapīṭha*) is the Śrīcakra, which is non-different from their own bodies; there, they gladden— that is, they worship with offerings such as *tarpaṇa*— the Deity together with the surrounding retinue (*sāvaraṇa*), using substances that have been turned into nectar (*sudhā*) by being drenched in it, and they rejoice.
Having first lost the appearance of objective objects,

they possess a non-conceptual mental state (*nirvikalpa-vṛtti*) whose sole object is their own Self. They dwell upon the summit of the great heaven and enter the supreme abode of the three cities (*traipura*).
This is the meaning. The "rendering immortal" (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) is an indicative mark for other consecratory rites (*saṃskāra*);
furthermore, that the presiding deity is the goddess Sudhā and that there is consciousness (*saṃvit*) [of this] is understood from the wording of the consecration mantra.

"Purified by the refinement of mantra, it is called the nectar of the deity. Thus, in the Rudrayāmala, it is said that the dwelling upon the great back of the celestial vault (nākapṛṣṭha) is indicative of the fruits of the three types of human goals; it is the supreme abode of Tripurā.
But its true nature is that which is to be approached by the liberated;
by that, liberation is spoken of, meaning that they attain all desires and liberation—this is the sense. Thus, that omnipresent power is discerned as Brahman.
The wise have declared that [the path] is of two kinds: with attributes (saguṇa) and without attributes (nirguṇa).
That with attributes is to be practiced by those possessed of passion, while that without attributes is for those free from passion.
She is the untroubled mistress of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa; when worshipped according to the prescribed rites, she grants all desired objects.

Thus it is also remembered in the *Devībhāgavata*. One initiated into the *Śrīvidyā* [attains the goal] through the worship of one's own seat (*svapīṭha*) with material offerings, by means of a state of non-conceptual mental modification (*nirvikalpakavṛtti*).

The injunction results in the prescription of another meditation characterized by meditation, namely: "One should meditate upon all desires. In every respect, the wise person should be initiated, and so forth.
This very scriptural statement is the source for the injunctions regarding the specific qualifications found in the *Kalpasūtras* and other texts.

Although the phrase "having understood, they satisfy" (*vijñāya tarpayantaḥ*) is heard as a qualification of the qualified agent (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*), the act of satisfying (*tarpaṇa*) is connected as the instrument (*karaṇa*) of the cultivation of the result (*phalabhāvanā*). [As it is said: "The givers of gold [attain] immortality."
Just as in the case of [the word] *bhajante*, because it expresses a meaning not yet established and because there is no obstruction to the power of injunction (*vidhi-śakti*),
there is no contradiction with its status as an injunction (*vidhitva*), even though it is a mantra. For the spring...
One should sacrifice *kapiñjala* birds, bringing forward those that are seeking [food] and are to be restrained;

for even in the case of mantras such as "Those who know from the mouth, not at all... and so forth, there is frequent acceptance of their status as injunctions (*vidhi*), just as in the case of the sentence concerning the *āgneya* offering, where the word "boiling" (*madantī*) functions as an injunction.

By the excellence of the *leṭ* [subjunctive] mood, according to the logic of the section on the meaning of verbal roots (*bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*), the very meaning of the root *mad*— which denotes a specific mental modification (*vṛtti*) whose object is solely one's own self as non-different from the Goddess of Consciousness—
is itself the instrument (*karaṇa*). This is also what is expressed by the term "inner sacrifice" (*antaryāga*).

Because that very root *yajati* (to sacrifice) expresses a specific mode of operation, the term *parisrutā* connects with the meaning of the verbal root through the indication of possessive significance (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*),

or else [it connects] with both [the root-meaning and the productive energy] when they are already connected to the productive energy (*bhāvanā*), according to the principle of the "red one-year-old cow" (*aruṇaikahāyanī-nyāya*).
The subsequent [passages] are to be connected with "they stand firm. For [the passage] beginning with "on the back of the firmament" (nākasya pṛṣṭhe) serves to present the result;
this is because the word "and" (ca) indicates a conjunction of results, as in: "He becomes indeed purified, radiant, an eater of food, and possessed of sensory power."

"May He who impels the intellect from within inspire us."

He distinguishes [the Self] from desire— that desire which, as established in the section on "Icchati" (Icchādhikaraṇa), is presented by the Śruti as "May I be many, may I procreate"—

The one who is to be described as the author of the Vedas and known through the Vedas— whose identity as the Supreme Brahman alone was stated in the two sections of the *Śāstrayonitvādhikaraṇa*—

And according to the tradition, the option is indeed optional.

Although the extraction (*uddhāra*) of other vidyās worshipped by Manu, Candra, and others is also seen in the *Tripurātāpinī*, in the present context, the extraction of only these two is given for the purpose of intimating their superiority. For this very reason, it is said in the *Jñānārṇava*:

This is further supported by such passages as these. Furthermore, because the *Kādividyā* alone is extracted first among these two as well (p.
23), there is an implied suggestion of its superiority; for this very reason—
"Among mantras, Śrīvidyā alone is supreme; therein, the Kadi-mantra is like the Aparā.

This is the expansion of the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*. In reality, however, because there is no difference between all the Vidyās, this statement regarding their relative gradation is merely for the sake of praise.

For this very reason, the venerable Ācārya Bhagavatpāda demonstrated the reversal of these two in the *Saundaryalaharī*. There too:

In order to conform to the context of the present scripture (*prakṛta-śruti*), the alternative interpretations of the terms *śiva*, *śakti*, and *kāma* offered by some should not be respected, as they are both strained and devoid of meaning; for here, it is the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*) alone that constitutes the subject matter (*prakaraṇa*).

Since the combination of other qualities by way of restating those very substances will be prescribed in the twelfth verse, it must be stated that the context continues; therefore, [this applies] to the *japa* occurring within that interval.

Because they are subordinate members of the internal sacrifice within the context (*prakaraṇa*), the statement "they partake in immortality" is an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise), just like the hearing of the "fame of the sinless. However, although the passage beginning with "tisraḥ puraḥ" is supplementary to the injunction for the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*), it does not constitute a mere explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*).

There is no evidence that being a supplement to an injunction (*vidhiśeṣatva*) is pervaded by being an explanatory passage (*arthavādatva*); furthermore, even if it were an explanatory passage, it would possess authority regarding its own meaning by virtue of being an explanatory passage stating an existing fact (*bhūtārthavāda*). Nor is the meditation on the "gross" (*sthūla-upāsti*) in the twelfth verse something entirely different.

It must be stated that it is prescribed as having the form of an external sacrifice; nevertheless, because the conclusion is seen in the fifteenth ṛc through the explanation of the meaning of the verbal root *dhā* (to place), the continuity of the context is unavoidable. In reality, [this applies] to the triad of meditations (*upāsti*).

There is indeed equal primacy; for even among the three injunctions, since a fruit is heard in each, there is no decisive criterion (*vinigamanā*) for designating any one of them as the primary context (*prakaraṇin*). Furthermore, like the group of six sacrifices beginning with the Āgneya, it is only when they are combined that they produce the result.
A householder should always perform both internal and external sacrifice:
the worship of the King of Wheels (Cakrarāja), the recitation of the Goddess’s mantra, and the chanting of Her names.
For a devotee, this much is the duty; they know anything else to be worldly prosperity.

This is because of such statements. The reasoning beginning with "like the establishment of the fruit" (*phalasiddhivat*) and so forth should be inferred by those learned in logic. Thus ends the ninth verse. Now, with the desire to teach the worship of the gross form (*sthūlopāsti*), [the author describes] the specific gross form for the purpose of establishing within the external *cakra* the Root Deity who has been meditated upon as possessing attributes (*saguṇa*) internally.
He speaks the tenth ṛc in order to explain it.
I praise that which is the triple heaven, the triple-faced, situated within the nine lines and the vowels of the Universal Mother.

The great lunar days (*bṛhattithi*), numbering fifteen beginning with the tenth, sustain that city of the Sixteenth (*ṣoḍaśī*) as the triple heaven (*triviṣṭapa*). Following the square of the lines, there is the elision (*praśleṣa*) of the vowel *visarga* of the sixteenth. Within the nine lines—the nine *ghaṭikās* of the womb (*yoni*)—is the syllable *aḥ*.
Thus, that which has the middle [position] corresponding to the vowel *a*; or, that which has nine lines—that is, the *saṃhāracakra*—and whose middle position is characterized by the vowel *a*;
or, that in which the vowel itself is the syllable *aḥ*.
Alternatively, the analysis [of the compound] is *aḥ-ravara*; such is the three-faced triangle—
meaning the central triangle— which is the triple-heaven (*triviṣṭapa*), the dwelling place, or rather the site of worship, of Viśvamātā Tripurasundarī.

Because heaven (*svarga*) is the abode of the deities, the place is indicated here by the word denoting that [heaven]. "Tadīle"—this is the statement of the praiser; and having reached the middle between these two vowels, the *saṅkāra* becomes the letter *la*. Thus.
By the rule of the *Prātiśākhya*, the letter *ḍa* has become *la*.

This very *Upaniṣad* is also recited by the followers of the *Atharvaveda*; according to their view, there is the established rule that it is not a substitute for a "badly articulated" (*dusspṛṣṭa*) sound. This is precisely because it is stated to have a middle tone (*madhyama*).

By the principle that "the others [are treated] equally because they are heard as such," the fifteen remaining vowels are divided fivefold and established in groups of five; this is indicated by the three lines being equal to the dot (bindu). That large triangle is thus manifested.

The meaning is that one should worship the fifty deities of the lunar days— the five groups of ten lunar days, beginning with Kāmeśvarī and ending with Citrā— as the eternal Nityās, each group of five being worshipped in its respective place along the southern, upper, and northern lines.
Having augmented that [in the heart] and visualized it in the ocean of knowledge,
one should subsequently draw five lines upon the great triangle in the sequence of the foremost, the right, and the left, according to the order of fives.
One should visualize the letters beginning with 'a' and ending with 'ra' on the southern line;
then, on the eastern line, the five [letters] beginning with 'dīrghakarṇa'.
Having inscribed [the letters] on the northern line, one should then inscribe Śakti and the others;
in the middle, ending with the Anusvāra and including the Visarga, one should worship the Ṣoḍaśī. Thus it is said.
The fifteen digits characterized by the waxing and waning of the moon are indeed the lunar days (tithis),
beginning with the new moon (darśa) and ending with the full moon (pūrṇimā); these digits are exactly fifteen.

These are indicated in the Tantra by such passages as [the list beginning with] "seeing, not-seeing, and non-seeing," and they are also recited by the Taittirīyas [in the *Taittirīya Āraṇyaka*]. It should be understood that it is logical for the sixteenth vowel to have that as its essence, because it manifests the letter *ha*, which consists of the forms of *prakāśa* (light) and *vimarśa* (reflective awareness).

If it is argued that, according to the injunctions situated within the section on sacrifices (*kratu-prakaraṇa*) in the *Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava*, this meditation is also remembered as being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), what follows from that? [The answer is:

Various kinds of foods consisting of mung beans and so forth. The fourth "place of origin" (*yonipada*) is an indicator for those born from a *kuṇḍa* or *golaka* womb; that is the fifth.

This refers to the intention of a few specific types of *jāti*.

That expansion [of the meaning] should be seen in the Tantras through such terms as the "eight *kalās*. The word "and" (*ca*) is intended to include all five together. Although *pala* is recited after *jhaṣa*, [it is to be understood here].

Because they are placed at the beginning by the first word prior to *jhaṣa*, the intended sequence of the *makāras* is indicated. Therefore, according to the principle that one may perform worship with substitutes when the primary items are unavailable,
the regular sequence (*nityakrama*) is maintained even if the five *makāras* are not obtained.

And although [the goal] is accomplished by means of the Kalpasūtra, it is indicated that if the preceding [means] are unavailable, one does not take up the succeeding primary [means], even if it is available.

Even when only the first measure is obtained, since the fourth is necessary for the purpose of the *naivedya* offering, taking that much alone is to be understood through the traditional practice (*sampradāya*). In the reading from another recension (*śākhā*) which says "clarified butter" (*ājyam*), the meaning is simply ghee; in that case, it is so because it means "cooked."

The qualification applies to both [the *tantra* and the *vikāra*] according to the maxim of the crow’s eye (*kākākṣigolakanyāya*).
