and because it would result in a restrictive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyā*) of the fivefold and other categories mentioned in the Sūtra.

Even if one obtains only enough for the mere act of satiating the Supreme Deity, the sacrifice is not performed by means of a substitute; for in an external sacrifice, since self-identification is a form of disposal (*pratipatti*),
there is no obstacle even if that [self-identification] is omitted, and so forth.
This should be inferred based on the logic established in the sixth [chapter]. They are well-refined, purified by both visible and invisible consecrations (*saṃskāra*);
and these are of two kinds: worldly, such as cooking and the like, and Vedic, such as the removal of curses and the like.
Many are well-known in the tantras.

Whether much or little, according to the maxim "as prescribed for one's own household," offering only as much as stated in the *Kalpasūtras* while presenting it to the Great Goddess, Mahādevī; the performer of the sacrifice, being a doer of good deeds who performs the external rite, having internalized those offerings within himself.
Having himself also consumed [the offering], he attains— that is, reaches— *siddhi*, the fruit of the sacrifice;

one should contemplate the attainment of the desired *siddhi* through a sacrifice dedicated to the deity Mahādevī, which possesses the fivefold sequence beginning with the first [syllable] as mutually combined.
The manner of concluding the ritual procedure and so forth should be understood as being exactly like the procedure for the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*).
The author recites the eighty-third verse in order to teach that meditation on the deity with attributes (*saguṇadhyāna*) is an auxiliary part of the sacrifice (*kratvaṅga*).
Like two dogs with a leash, the one who moves among all people binds those who approach him with a noose. With five arrows and a bow,
the innate power, ruddy and beloved by all, pierces them.

"Like a goad with a white [tip]" (*sṛṇyeva sitayā*). The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used here in the sense of a characteristic mark (*itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇa*). She is characterized by a goad (*sṛṇyā*), that is, a hook (*aṅkuśa*), which is white—that is, made of silver—or, because of the non-difference between "white" and "sharpened," by one that is sharpened, meaning it has a keen edge. She is thus distinguished by such a goad.

Viśvajanyā—she from whom all that is born arises; the mother of the entire universe, Aruṇā, possessing a crimson luster, the primordial power Mahātripurasundarī; Viśvacarṣaṇi—the beholder of the auspicious and inauspicious deeds of every living being; [she who bestows grace upon] those who long for her.
He binds with a snare those who are lustful and, driven by craving and greed, proceed along this path;
having bound them with the snare, he pierces them with a bow and five arrows.

It causes those who are devoid of craving to fall downward; however, as for the fact that it leads upward those who proceed by means of discriminative wisdom, this is already established by the injunction itself and thus is not stated again.
As it has been said:
One should practice [the path] with the understanding that it is a prescribed injunction; if one serves it out of craving, one is a sinner.
By those very same substances through which downfall occurs, liberation is likewise impelled.
"Of the one who is not afraid and of the one who is afraid—thus these are established," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "like a goad" (*sṛṇyeva*), Yāska states that the goad is of two kinds: the supporter and the slayer.
The word "like" (*iva*), being connected everywhere, [indicates] the form endowed with qualities (*saguṇarūpa*).

By characterizing [the form] as a conceptualization for the sake of bestowing grace upon devotees, it reveals that the form devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) alone is the ultimate reality. Precisely because the form with qualities (saguṇa) is a conceptualization,
the fourteenth verse is spoken in order to teach the equal primacy of both the female and the male.
Bhaga is power (śakti).

(14) Bhaga is power, and the Blessed One is desire; both are lords and givers here of fortunes. They are equal in preeminence, equal in essence, equal in fearlessness, and equal in power—the undecaying source of the universe.
"Bhaga" is a synonym for "Vimarsa" (reflective awareness); it is defined as the sixfold [perfection] consisting of complete sovereignty, virtue, fame, fortune, knowledge, and discernment.

By such Smṛti passages as these, the entire aggregate of attributes that constitutes the nature of Īśvara is indicated here by the word *bhaga*; such a collection of attributes alone is called *śakti*. [This refers to] the female form described as the object of worship.

This is the true nature of the deity. As it is stated in the *Nāgānanda-sūtra*, having introduced the self-reflection (*vimarśa*) which constitutes the very nature of Brahman whose essence is light: "This indeed..."

Discernment (*vimarśa*), consciousness (*citi*), sentience (*caitanya*), the Self (*ātman*), that which arises by its own inherent nature (*svarasodita*), the Supreme Speech (*parāvāk*), the orientation toward the Supreme Self as absolute freedom (*svātantrya-paramātmaunmukhya*), sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), true reality (*sat-tattva*), existence (*sattā*), radiance (*sphurattā*), the essence (*sāra*), *Mātṛkā*, and *Mālinī*.
The wave of the heart is the vibration of one's own consciousness.
Thus it is proclaimed by such scriptural authorities as these.
A detailed exposition of these specific attributes of Dharma is to be found in its commentary (*bhāṣya*) itself.

The Blessed One is indeed distinguished by such a collection of qualities. He is the Lord of Desire (*kāmeśvara*), for this alone is the masculine form of the deity to be worshipped. Herein, through worship, there is the attainment of fortunes consisting of virtue (*dharma*), wealth (*artha*), and desire (*kāma*).

The meaning is that both are bestowers of various fruits; even through the twofold meditation on the qualities of a single deity, the accomplishment of the three aims of life (*trivarga*) is attained.

The term *sattva* here refers to the *guṇas*; thus, they are of equal primacy and equal essence, meaning they have entered into a mutual relationship of attribute (*guṇa*) and substrate (*guṇin*). Śiva is the *guṇa* because, in meditation, he serves as the substratum by virtue of being the seat upon which Kāmeśvarī rests.

Śakti is the primary [element], because in meditation upon Śiva as joined with Ambikā— who is half of him— she constitutes specific limbs such as the hands and head; thus, Śakti is the attribute (guṇa),
while the sense is that Śiva alone is the primary [substance].

Thus, although there is equality in the capacity to bestow the desired fruit and in the mutual relationship of subordinate and predominant qualities, the aspect of being the creator of the world resides solely in Śakti; therefore,
indicating that the attainment of the fruit is swift through meditation on her very form as a woman, he says:

Regarding the phrase "of the two alone": it refers to the Goddess herself, who possesses equal power, whose power is universal, and who consists of the entire aggregate of attributes, situated between Śiva and Śakti in the form of Ardhanārīśvara, being perfectly merged (*ota*) with one another without distinction.
She is the source of the universe and the protectress of the world. Accordingly, the Śaktisūtra states:

"Consciousness is autonomous and the cause of the manifestation of the universe. The word *sama* is well-known as a synonym for "all" (*sarva*), as seen in such passages as *uruṣyāṇo aghāyataḥ samasmāt* ("May he protect us from every one who intends evil"). [The term] *ajarā*...

Regarding the aspect of being the source of the universe (*viśvayonitva*), the qualification "being the creator of the world" is accepted because it is free from the stain of doubt, as it is established by means of valid cognition such as direct perception; this is what is meant. As it is stated in the *Bhāgavata*:
Śakti creates the universe; she alone protects it entirely;
by her will, she destroys this world of moving and unmoving beings.
Neither Viṣṇu, nor Hara, nor Indra, nor Brahmā, nor Agni [is its creator].
Neither Ārka nor Varuṇa were able to accomplish their respective tasks in any way whatsoever.
"For joined with her, those gods perform their respective duties;
she alone is the cause in their actions, as is perceived through direct observation. Thus [it is said].
Even Śiva elsewhere becomes a corpse when deprived of Kuṇḍalinī;
whoever is devoid of power is considered by the wise to be incapable.

Such details are to be seen in the *Setubandha*. Therefore, although Śiva possesses the capacity to bestow fruits and so forth, this is delayed because it is dependent upon Śakti; however, for Śakti...

The sense is that because it is independent [of external aids], it is "unhesitating"; therefore, for those desiring swift accomplishment, it is appropriate to meditate on the deity specifically in female form. Having thus explained meditation on the qualified (saguṇa), since there is no further portion to be stated regarding meditation on the unqualified (nirguṇa), [the author speaks of] its resulting fruit.
And in order to teach the channel for its production, he recites the fifteenth verse,
beginning with "parisrutā."
(15) When the mind has dissolved from the contraction [of egoism] through the purified sacrificial offering of the flowing liquor, it becomes liberated.
Everyone is the creator, the sustainer, and the destroyer of the entire world; thus one attains the state of universal form.
Regarding the paths of action (*karmamārga*), the path of knowledge (*jñānamārga*), and the path of devotion (*bhaktimārga*),
various indirect means (*praṇāḍikā*) distinct from one another have been taught by the founders of their respective scriptures; all of these [are as follows].
That "difficult-to-acquire [merits] yield fruits over a long period of time" is indeed clear to those who know the various scriptures. In this context,
however, the channel [of attainment] is simply a succession of exhilarations produced by the repeated acceptance of substances.

In that regard, the duties prescribed by the conventional conduct (*samayācāra*) apply up to the limit of the matured outpouring (*prauḍhollāsa*); at the end of that outpouring, there is freedom of action (*yāthākāmya*); and in the final outpouring, there is the nature of Brahman itself.

And so says the Kalpasūtra: "In the stages of the commencement of youth, tender youth, mature youth, the end of maturity, and the overflowing of the mind beyond that, the practice of the rule (samayācāra) extends up to the end of maturity; after that, one may act according to desire (yathākāmī)."

The definitions of the seven joys (*ullāsa*) are to be found in the *Kulārṇava* and other such texts. Although the attainment of the nature of Brahman indeed occurs every day during the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*),
this is because at that time the mind has dissolved.

Nevertheless, because it is permeated by sleep—which is a specific transformation of ignorance—that state is not the goal of human life (*puruṣārtha*). However, such a state when devoid of sleep is indeed the goal of human life; it is that which is designated as the seventh stage among the stages of knowledge (*jñānabhūmikā*).

The wise consider that what yogis experience as the state of non-conceptual absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*) is precisely that which is experienced by yogis even during the expansion of the state beyond the Unstruck Sound (*unmanottara-avasthā*). As it has been said:
"Bliss is the form of Brahman, and that is established within the body;
the substance that manifests it is drunk by the yogis. Thus [it is said].
In the Kalpasūtra, however,
it is stated that its manifestors are the five *makāras*.

However, if that very same substance, being an auxiliary part of a sacrifice, is impure when drunk, then— being obstructed by the sin arising from the inclination toward what is prohibited for a person— it is not capable of producing that [intoxicating] state; [provided it has been] purified by mantras.
Rather, it is the very form of the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) that produces the state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*). This has been stated in the *Samayācārasmṛti*:
"The unrefined drink of a bound soul (*paśu*) causes strife, agitation, and sin."
Indeed, that which is devoid of mantra and worship is merely the drinking of blood by a beast.
Even a hero, having drunk according to the rite of animal-sacrifice liquor (paśupāna), would go to hell;
however, that which produces awakening when consecrated is the expiation that effects purification.
Through that radiance of the mantras, great sins are destroyed;
by drinking [the nectar] consecrated [by them], one gains longevity, prosperity, beauty, good fortune, and knowledge.

The eightfold sovereignty, the power of moving through the sky, and falling [from it] according to the prescribed rule; (p. 34) in the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice and in the Kula practice, a Brāhmaṇa may drink wine;
elsewhere, having drunk it, a Brāhmaṇa must perform an expiation.

And so forth. However, it is better that one's life-breaths depart than that a Brāhmaṇa should offer liquor; for by drinking intoxicating liquor, a Brāhmaṇa falls away from his very status as a Brāhmaṇa.
Because this has been prohibited by such statements as those from the *Śaktisaṃgamatantrarāja* and other scriptures,
the means for casting off the fetters of dharma (*dharmapāśa*) here must be understood solely through the oral tradition (*sampradāya*).

The various modes of systematic arrangement have been demonstrated by us in the *Kaulopaniṣadbhāṣya*. Consequently, for those who possess such qualification, through such exultations, [the state of] that which is delimited by the internal organ—
When the contraction of the individual soul (jīvātman) caused by the limiting adjunct of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is removed,
what remains upon its becoming Brahman?
Nor can one achieve the goal of life merely through that [state], since the manifestation of the substance is subject to coming and going.

It must be stated that this objection applies equally even to the case of meditative absorption (samādhi). Now, in that case, through means such as the regulation of breath (pavana-niyamana) and by entering into absorption again and again, one attains proficiency through long-term practice; consequently, after a few days have passed, [the result occurs] even without [external effort].
If it is argued that "the cessation of the breath gives rise to a concentration (*samādhi*) that persists at all times,

just as we observe that for those traveling by boat upon the ocean who have been rocked for a long time by its waves, the rocking continues even after they have disembarked," then the same [objection] applies.
The same applies to the subject at hand as well.

Even without the substance, such an unartificial state is accomplished within a few days through proficiency in the practice of the state of *unmanī* born from the drinking of the refined substance (*saṃskṛtadravyapāna*). As for the literal meaning of the word, it is [attained] by means of that which has been purified (*pāvitena*).

When the contraction of the self— the sense of limitation arising from the internal organ (*manas*)— has dissolved and melted away without re-emergence, through the oblation (*havis*) consecrated by mantra-refinement, which remains as the residue of the Goddess’s worship and is being consumed as *parisrut* liquor; and when that contraction has vanished from the mind.

This means: in the state that transcends the expansion of *unmanī*. Indeed (*vai*), with certainty, everyone becomes the self of all. Therefore, intoxication (*mada*) is that which generates a non-conceptual mental state (*nirvikalpa-vṛtti*) whose sole object is one's own nature.

Thus, in the sentence prescribing the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*), it is concluded that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is what is intended. With this very intention, the manifold nature of what is established in the *Tantra* is demonstrated.
"Those who lust enjoy themselves when intoxicated; those who are prone to anger become angry when intoxicated;
singers sing when intoxicated; and yogis meditate when intoxicated. Thus it is said.
By this, a specific yoga is also implied as being an auxiliary to this [state]. He explains his very nature as the self of all:
he alone is Brahmā, the creator of the entire world; Viṣṇu, its sustainer;
and Rudra, its destroyer. What need is there for more?
He says that he himself becomes the very form of every living being, such as a slave, a fisherman, or a Kaitava, by stating:

"he attains the state of universal form. As for the falling away of the body, let it happen whenever and wherever it may due to the force of *prārabdha* karma; it does not matter to him [in the least].
What is the distinction? The sense is that [he] has accomplished all that was to be done (*kṛtakṛtyatva*). And it is said in the *Kalpasūtra*:

"Having understood this and having performed [the rites] according to rule, for one who is devoted to his lineage, there is a state of having accomplished all duties in every respect; upon the casting off of the body, there is no difference between the house of a dog-eater and Kāśī."
"He is called liberated while living."
Thus, concluding the exposition of the Tri-pura Siddhānta, he recites this sixteenth verse ending in *yajus* in order to teach that there is also fruit from its study: "This... [iyaṃ].
"The Great Upaniṣad."

(16) This is the Great Upaniṣad of Tripurā, whose imperishable syllable is praised with supreme words. She is the Ṛg, she is the Yajus, she is the supreme Sāman, she is this Atharvan, and she is every other branch of knowledge. Thus ends the Upaniṣad.
And this has been further augmented by the venerable Śrī Paraśurāma, the author of the Kalpasūtra, who said: "He who studies this Daśama-khaṇḍī Mahopaniṣad,
which constitutes the very essence of the great Tri-pura Siddhānta, [attains] in all..."
"He becomes a performer of sacrifices in all sacrifices; whatever ritual he studies, by that very one his sacrifice is performed"—so indeed it is heard in the Upaniṣad. May there be auspiciousness.
p.36) By this [principle],

those meanings required but not explicitly stated in this Mahopaniṣad are to be taken from the Kalpasūtras; for in the section concerning the Kalpasūtras, [it is established] according to the different Vedic branches (*śākhā*).
Thus it is established that the authority of the *prayoga-śāstra* (treatise on ritual performance) is supported only with respect to those who are capable of collecting the scattered [Vedic] verses.
As for the literal meaning: this *Mahopaniṣad* of Tripurā, which consists of a collection of sentences revealing the secret [teachings], is to be recited—this is the ellipsis.
He states the reasons for this with the words beginning "yām" (which...), [referring to] the Supreme Imperishable, Brahman, as the agent.
This Upanishad which one praises with words—that is, with words of praise; *riṭṭe* is the form of the root *riḍ*, meaning "to praise. In the word *parame*, *so* is substituted for *saḥ*.
[The name is formed] by the transposition of the two words *yām* and *brahma*.
Or rather, it is a hymn (*stu-ti*) composed by the Upanishads, having Brahman as its object, by virtue of accepting [the text] as ending in the nominative and accusative cases;
the meaning is that this is because it is praised even by the Supreme Lord and because it is laudatory of Him. [She who is] Tripurā, whose syllable is *hṛllekhā*...
Or it means "he praises. Alternatively, there is a word-division as "paraṃ e," meaning the syllable in the form of the letter *e*.
As it is said: "That seed-syllable which is the eleventh support, arising from the three corners, is seen even today as the entire world, from the Egg of Brahmā down to the outer shell."
Because of the scriptural statement:
"Even in the letter *e*, there is a division into *a* and *i*;
for all speech is indeed in space (*ākāśa*), as the Śruti says: 'If he hears *iṃ*, he hears *alaka*.'"

Alternatively, the final *oṃkāra* is construed as qualifying the word "syllable" (*akṣara*). The meaning is: "He, though supreme and indivisible, praises her with words—that is, with the syllables *a*, *u*, and *m*."
"Whether taken collectively or individually, one who praises the refuge [of Śiva] utters the word 'Om'";
thus it is remembered in the *Śivarahasya*. Furthermore, there are various studies prescribed by the injunction "one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) must be studied."

He says "this" (*eṣā*) to show that [the results] are accomplished by the study of this very [text]. The words *ṛk* and so forth refer to the Vedas as a whole, and not to individual mantras, because they occur in a context primarily consisting of the Atharvan and others.
The words *eṣā*, *etat*, and *ayam* refer to the *Ṛg*, *Yajus*, and *Atharvaṇa* [Vedas].
This is with the intention of [the Sāman] being the qualificand. Since the Sāman consists of sound and thus lacks syllables (*anakṣara*),
the phrase "as it were" (*iva*) indicates that the syllables yield a fruit equal to that [of the Sāman].
By taking four out of the eighteen branches of learning (*vidyā*), the other fourteen, such as the *Upavedas* and so forth, are understood by the word "others."
The meaning is that this Upaniṣad is the very essence of all sounds.
He states "Om" to show that this [Upaniṣad] is also the very essence of the Praṇava. By the rule *omāṅośca*, there is a single substitute (pararūpa);
thus, the intention is that it should be recited even by ascetics (*yatins*).
With the intention that "such is this Upaniṣad," for one who knows its greatness,
even the Śruti itself is unable to directly express its greatness,
because it is of the singular nature of Brahman and words do not function therein; thus says the Śruti.
"It is the Upanishad established in silence"—the sense is that there is no further secret portion to be spoken beyond this. Thus [ends] the Śrī.
Thus, by Bhāskararāya, who has piled the sacrificial fires, certain meanings of the Tripurā Mahopaniṣad—
which though unfit to be made public, have been told here for the satisfaction of the learned.
Thus ends the commentary on the Tripuropaniṣad composed by the illustrious Mahāśaya Bhāskararāya.
"May my speech be in my mind"—thus [ends] the peace invocation.
The Śrī Lalitā Mahātripurasundarī Upaniṣad.
The Goddess, belonging to the Bahvṛca-veda, sat with one-pointed concentration. She alone created the cosmic egg; she is known as Kāmakalā and is known as Śṛṅgārakalā. From her alone Brahmā was born.
Viṣṇu brought it forth; Rudra brought it forth; all the hosts of Maruts brought it forth;
the Gandharvas, Apsarases, and Kinnaras, playing upon musical instruments, brought it forth from every side;
they brought forth that which is to be enjoyed; they brought forth everything; they brought forth everything consisting of Śakti.

Whatever is born from an egg, born from sweat, born from a sprout, or born from a womb—whatever living being exists, whether stationary or moving, including human beings—this is that Supreme Power (Parāśakti). This is that Śāmbhavī Vidyā; it is known as the Kādi Vidyā or the Hādi Vidyā.

Whether it be called *vidyā* or *sādi*, whether it be called *vidyā* or *rahasya*; Oṃ Oṃ! Established in speech, she pervades the three cities and the three bodies, illuminating both the external and the internal.
Due to her non-attachment to space, time, and objects, she is indeed Mahātripurasundarī, the inward-facing consciousness (*pratyak-citi*).

That alone is the Self; everything other than that is unreal and non-Self. Therefore, this realization of Brahman is free from the categories of existence and the act of being; it is the primordial consciousness, the non-dual realization of Brahman, a wave of Being-Consciousness-Bliss.
Mahātripurasundarī, having entered within and without, shines forth as herself alone.
That which exists is pure Being (sanmātra); that which shines is pure Consciousness (cinmātra); that which is dear is Bliss (ānanda).
She who is all these forms is Mahātripurasundarī. You and I are all this.
The universe consists of all the deities; everything else is Mahātripurasundarī. Truth is the single reality known as Lalitā; she is the non-dual, indivisible supreme Brahman.
p.40) Through the abandonment of the five forms and the relinquishing of non-essential nature,
the supreme substratum— the one great Reality— remains as the true [Self].
It is expressed as "Consciousness is Brahman," or "I am Brahman.
It is indeed addressed as "That thou art. Or it is said: "This Self is Brahman," or "I am indeed Brahman," or "Whoever I am, that I am," or "I am that."
That which is expressed as "I am He" (yo'sau so'hamasmi) is this very sixteenfold Śrīvidyā,
the fifteen-syllabled Mahātripurasundarī; she is known as Bālāmbikā, or Bagalā, or Mātaṅgī, or Svayaṃvarakalyāṇī, or Bhuvaneśvarī.
She is Cāmuṇḍā, Caṇḍā, Vārāhī, Tiraskariṇī, Rājamātaṅgī,
Śukaśyāmā, Laghuśyāmā, Aśvārūḍhā, Pratyaṅgirā, Dhūmāvatī, Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, and Sarasvatī.
The bliss of Brahman is the kalā.

In the imperishable syllable of the Ṛgveda, in the supreme firmament, upon which all the gods have settled—whosoever does not know that, what will he do with the Ṛgveda? But those who know it, they sit here together.
Thus ends the Upaniṣad. "May my speech be in my mind"—thus is the peace invocation.
Thus ends the Lalitā-Mahātripurasundarī Upaniṣad belonging to the Bahvṛca Veda.
"Even those who recite the Atharvaveda attain the supreme goal," thus it is said in the Nāgara-khaṇḍa.
The Atharvaśīrṣa Upaniṣad of the Goddess.
Oṃ, "May we hear with our ears what is auspicious," thus is the peace invocation.

Oṃ. All the gods indeed approached the Goddess and said: "Who are you, O Great Goddess? She replied: "I am the embodiment of Brahman. From me proceeds the universe consisting of Prakṛti and Puruṣa; I am both the void and the non-void; I am bliss and non-bliss."
"I am consciousness and unconsciousness; I am Brahmā and the non-Brahmā; thus says the Atharvaṇa Śruti. I am the five elements and that which is not the five elements;
I am the entire universe. I am the Veda and the non-Veda; I am knowledge and ignorance."
I am the unborn, I am the un-born; I am below, above, and across.
I move with the Rudras and the Vasus; I move with the Ādityas and the Viśvedevas.
I support both Mitra and Varuṇa; I [support] Indra and Agni, and I [support] both the Aśvins.
I bestow Soma, Tvaṣṭṛ, Pūṣan, and Bhaga;
I bestow Viṣṇu of the wide stride, as well as Brahmā and Prajāpati.
I bestow wealth upon the one who offers oblations, the skillful sacrificer who presses the juice.

I am the sovereign ruler who gathers together all treasures; I bring forth the father upon the summit of this world. My source is within the waters, in the ocean. He who knows this attains the station of the Goddesses. Those gods said: "Homage to the Goddess, the Great Goddess!"
Constant salutation to Śivā! Salutation to Prakṛti, to Bhadrā;

we, being self-restrained, bow down to her. To that goddess Durgā, who is fire-colored, blazing with ascetic fervor, the daughter of Virocana, and who is honored for the fruits of actions—to her [we offer praise].

I take refuge in her who utterly destroys darkness—the Goddess Speech whom the gods brought forth; she whom creatures of every form speak. May that Cow, Speech, yielding for us pleasant food and vigor, protect us with her well-sounding praise.
We bow to Kālarātri, praised by Brahmā, the power of Viṣṇu, the mother of Skanda, Sarasvatī, Aditi, the daughter of Dakṣa—the purifying and auspicious one.
We know Mahālakṣmī; may we meditate upon all-perfecting success. May that Goddess [grant it] to us.

May she impel us. For Aditi was born, she who is your daughter, O Dakṣa. After her were born the gods, the auspicious ones whose kinship is with immortality. Kāma, Yoni, Kamalā, Vajrapāṇi, Guhā, Hasa, Mātariśvan, Abhra, Indra—and again, Guhā.
Furthermore, she who is the Mother of the Universe, possessing all the sciences beginning with the letter 'A', is the treasury of all through her power of illusion (*māyā*).
She is this very power of the Self (*ātma-śakti*), the deluder of the universe, bearing the noose, the goad, the bow, and the arrow; she is the illustrious *Mahāvidyā*. He who [knows her thus]...
One who knows this crosses over sorrow. Homage be to you, O Blessed One, O Bhavati, O Mother; protect us on every side. She is these eight Vasus;
she is these eleven Rudras; she is these twelve Ādityas; she is this—

The Viśvedevas are both drinkers of Soma and non-drinkers of Soma. This [universe] consists of Yātudhānas, Asuras, Rakṣasas, Piśācas, Yakṣas, and Siddhas. This is the [manifestation of] sattva, rajas, and tamas;
this is Prajāpati, Indra, and Manu. This is...
I perpetually bow to her who takes the form of time— consisting of the planets, constellations, luminaries, kalās, kāṣṭhās, and so forth; to the Goddess who removes all suffering,
who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, who is infinite, victorious, and pure.

The seed-syllable of the Goddess, which is the refuge, the bestower of auspiciousness, and auspicious itself; joined with the letter *i* (the sky) and the letter *ka* (fire), adorned with a crescent moon, and the accomplisher of all aims— such is the single-syllable mantra for ascetics.

Those of pure mind, consisting of supreme bliss and being oceans of knowledge, meditate upon Him; therefore, He is endowed with six faces, including the one whose nature is speech, illusion, and Brahman.

The Sun (Ra) joined with the left ear (Va) and the bindu (Ṃ), followed by the third letter of the ṭa-group (Ḍa); joined with Nārāyaṇa (Na), and Vāyu (Ya) joined with the lower lip (U). This nine-syllabled mantra should be known as the bestower of great bliss.
I worship her who dwells in the center of the heart-lotus, radiant as the morning sun, the daughter of Soma,
holding a noose and a goad, with hands granting boons and fearlessness, three-eyed, clad in red garments, and the fulfiller of the desires of her devotees. I bow to her.
I [praise] you, the Goddess, the destroyer of great fear.
She who pacifies great calamities and embodies supreme compassion; because her true nature is unknown even to Brahmā and the other gods, she is called "the unknowable" (Ajñeyā);
because her end is not found, she is called "the infinite" (Anantā); [and] because her grasping...

Because she is not perceived, she is called "unperceivable" (alakṣyā). Because her birth is not perceived, she is called "unborn" (ajā). Because she alone exists everywhere, she is called "one" (ekā). Because she alone possesses all forms, she is called "not one" (naikā). Therefore...
Thus she is called the unknowable, the infinite, the uncharacterizable, the unborn, the one, and the many.
She is Mātṛkā-devī of the mantras, the embodiment of knowledge of all words; she is beyond the consciousness of all cognitions, the witness of the void among all voids—she whose...
There is nothing higher than her; she is proclaimed as Durgā. Because she protects one from difficulties (durga), the Goddess is called Durgā. I take refuge in the Goddess;
O Dudurge, remove my misfortune! [I seek] that Goddess Durgā, who is difficult to attain.

I, fearing worldly existence, bow to her who destroys misconduct and carries one across the ocean of saṃsāra. Whoever studies this Atharvaśīrṣa obtains the fruit of reciting all five Atharvaśīrṣas. This is the Atharvaśīrṣa.

He who performs worship without knowing [this] does not attain success in that worship, even after reciting it a million times. One hundred and eight recitations of this is recorded as the rule for the preliminary rite (puraścaryā).
He who recites it ten times is immediately liberated from sins.
By the grace of the Great Goddess, one crosses over great difficulties.
Studying [this] in the evening, one destroys the sin committed during the day;
studying it in the morning, one destroys the sin committed during the night.
By practicing [this recitation] at dawn and dusk, one becomes free from sin;
by reciting it at midnight, during the fourth twilight (turīyasandhyā), mastery of speech is attained.
By reciting it before a newly consecrated image, the presence of the deity is established.
By reciting this during the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (the rite of consecrating the vital breaths), the establishment of the vital breaths occurs.

By reciting it on an Ashvinī day under the constellation Bhauma in the presence of Mahādevī, one who knows this thus crosses over great death. This is the Upanishad. Om, "With auspicious ears..."—thus the peace.
Oṃ tat sat.
Thus ends the Devyatharvaśīrṣa Upaniṣad.
The Śrī Kaulopaniṣad and its Commentary:
Oṃ! May the Kaulika be auspicious to us; may Vāruṇī be auspicious to us; may purity be auspicious to us;
may Agni be auspicious to us; may everything be auspicious to us. All became one.
Bhāskararāya, whose heart-coverings have been dispelled by the spreading rays from the lotus feet of his venerable guru,
causes the Kaulopaniṣad of the Atharvaveda to blossom.

In order to dispel the inevitable obstacles that arise when teaching the extremely secret matter about to be explained, he prays to the deities with the words beginning "May there be auspiciousness for us,
O Kaulika," and so forth.

May the Kaulika, the Supreme Śiva who is the initiator of the family path (kulamārga), who bestows the bliss of one's own self after first dispelling all obstacles— He who is the primary presiding deity of Vāruṇī— be present for us.
May the Great Deity also be auspicious to us; may the Deity presiding over purity, the second [tattva], also be auspicious to us;
may Agni, the fire, be so; and what need is there to say more—may everything be conducive to happiness.

Salutation to Brahman; salutation to the Earth; salutation to the Waters; salutation to Agni; salutation to Vāyu; salutation to the Gurus. You alone are the manifest [Brahman]; you indeed are she. I shall speak of you as the manifest; I shall speak of her; I shall speak the *ṛta*; I shall speak the truth.
I shall speak; may that protect me, may it protect the speaker; may it protect me, may it protect the speaker. Om. Peace, peace, peace.
Salutation to the Supreme Brahman, to the deities of the four elements beginning with earth, and to the lineage of gurus from Paramaśiva down to one's own teacher.

The four elements, as well as space, are implied; Brahman, which is directly perceived through the guise of the notion of "I" and is experienced by all—that very Brahman is you yourself. This is because [it is stated] in the *Kaulopaniṣad* concerning the form of Tripurasundarī: "Therefore, O..."

I shall declare you alone, who are non-different from that, as the Kaulopaniṣad. The word *ṛta* refers to Brahman; the word *satya* is likewise. The repetition [of the words] is for emphasis; the rest is clear. "Śāntiḥ śāntiḥ śāntiḥ"—this is a prayer for the pacification of obstacles.

Now, therefore, begins the inquiry into Dharma. Knowledge and wisdom are both termed "jñāna," and knowledge is the sole cause of liberation (mokṣa). Liberation is the realization of the identity of all selves. The five objects of the senses constitute phenomenal expansion (prapañca); their true nature is that of the Knower. Yoga is liberation.
Now, since the knowledge of the substratum has arisen immediately after the desire to know Brahman,
inquiry must be undertaken for the sake of knowing the attribute through the power of reflection upon it (this is the meaning).

"Knowledge (*jñāna*) and intellect (*buddhi*): direct experience of Brahman is *jñāna*, while that which produces it—verbal [knowledge]—is indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*), which is *buddhi*. That whose intellect proceeds toward reality until it culminates in direct experience... and so forth.

The meaning is that because both types of conventional usage are observed, both of these are indeed the very nature (*svarūpa*) of *dharma*. By the word "and" (*ca*), there is the inclusion of unmentioned attributes (*dharma*) such as consciousness (*caitanya*) and others which have been enumerated in works such as the *Nāgānanda*.
Acceptance. Knowledge is the sole cause of liberation; the meaning is clear.

Liberation is the realization of being the Self of all. Being the Self of all means the non-difference of everything from one's own Self; its realization is the cessation of ignorance along with its manifestations regarding that [Self]. Therefore, for the Bhāgavata consisting of half a verse as described in the Devībhāgavata, everything—
It is implied that the knowledge having the same meaning as "this alone is indeed the eternal [Self], there is nothing else" is the producer of liberation;
or rather, the undivided mental modification (*vṛtti*) produced by such knowledge.
He explains the term "all" by stating that the five sense-objects are the *prapañca*.
The pentad of sense-objects, beginning with sound, is denoted by the word *prapañca*,
because the gross elements are non-different from those subtle elements.
"Because even the thirty-six principles (tattvas) are included therein, the five elements exist everywhere, and there is nothing as a sixth. Thus it is stated in the Vāsiṣṭha.

Having thus indicated the class of insentient things by the phrase "whose nature is knowledge," he now indicates the class of sentient beings. "Jñāna" means one who knows and breathes—that is, one who cognizes objects and lives. The meaning is that living beings (jīvas) possess such a nature. "Yoga" refers to liberation (mokṣa).
Yoga is the cessation of mental fluctuations; liberation, too, is this.
Knowledge is indeed the absence of knowledge regarding the causes of unrighteousness.

Because it is devoid of attributes (*dharma*), *adharma* is the Supreme Brahman; that which is the causal ignorance regarding It is precisely the primordial ignorance (*mūlājñāna*) concerning knowledge—here the particle *eva* is displaced [in the compound]; the objects are the individual souls (*jīva*), and [their] union is...

The meaning is that all this—liberation, ignorance, and so forth—is nothing other than knowledge; there is no such thing as [duality] separate from Śakti. The implication is that duality is false. The manifest world (prapañca) is the Lord (īśvara), because even the relationship of the governed and the governor, which is pervaded by duality, [is likewise unreal].
Because it is false, by the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader,
the Lord is indeed the phenomenal world itself—
even things such as jars, which are impermanent, appear as permanent due to their impermanence.
It is indeed of the nature of eternal power;
ignorance is knowledge,
and even ignorance, being of the nature of a state, is indeed of the nature of knowledge.
The meaning is that it is indeed power (śakti).
Non-dharma itself is dharma.

Even dharma, which is of the nature of power (*śakti*), is not a separate category of reality (*padārthāntara*); rather, it is Brahman itself, appearing in the form of the substratum and its attributes.
This is liberation.
This alone is the path to liberation; there is no other.
The five bonds are of the nature of consciousness.
The notion of self in what is not-self, the notion of non-self in what is self, and so forth—such cognitions alone constitute bondage. This is because of the *Śivasūtra*: "Cognition is bondage.
Furthermore, there is the mutual differentiation among individual souls (*jīva*), the differentiation from the Lord (*īśvara*), and the differentiation from pure consciousness (*caitanya*).
Thus, there are five together with the three types of knowledge.
Birth from a lump of flesh.
It is precisely because of the existence of such bondage that birth, which consists in connection with the microcosmic egg (piṇḍāṇḍa), occurs.
Liberation is found in that very state.
However, by the power of the knowledge of the Kaula (kaulajñāna), even liberation occurs right there, within that very physical body (piṇḍāṇḍa);

there is no longer any delay in the form of the departure through more than a hundred channels, the journey on the path of the gods (devayāna), or liberation together with Brahmā. For him, it lasts only so long...
For a long time; "his vital breaths do not depart," and so forth, according to another Vedic scripture.
This is knowledge.
Having first stated the established tenets of the scripture, he declares the essence of knowledge: "this" refers to the treasury of all knowledge that is about to be described.
Among all the sense faculties, the eye is the foremost.

One should lead back to Brahman. Even in the individual cognitions produced by all six sense organs, which take the form "I know this" and so forth, it is Brahman alone appearing as the "I" that is the primary element. That very [Brahman]—

For the Śruti states, "Everything shines only after it has shone," thereby declaring that everything other than That also shines only by its light. One should strive so that such discrimination occurs in all mental functions (vṛttis), even those produced by a single sense organ.
One should lead the primary element (pradhāna) by means of knowledge through the mantra of discernment.
"Since all embodied beings possess the same general awareness of the grasped and the grasper,
this distinction [of the yogi] lies solely in his attentiveness toward the relationship [between them]. According to this statement,
the meaning is that the very absence of non-discrimination is the entire essence of knowledge.
Actions contrary to the Dharma should not be performed.
From this point forward, he instructs on the manner in which a lay practitioner (*upāsaka*) should act.

For the sake of stabilizing the mind and so forth of those who take singular delight in being the locus of such discerning knowledge, one should practice the service of *saṃvit* and the rest even during the time of ritual action.
It is proper to act in a manner that does not contradict the Dharmaśāstras.
Those who perform actions contrary to the Dharma are not to be associated with.
Even the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices prescribed by the Dharmaśāstras are appropriate to perform when there is a possibility of such an obstruction to the stream [of practice].
This is an authorization for both doing and not doing, and not an absolute injunction or prohibition; likewise, even by Gautama,
the forty sacraments (saṃskāras) were enumerated.

Having described the eight external and internal [disciplines], it was stated that after internal purification, the external ones are no longer necessary. Likewise, Manu, after describing all duties in detail, prescribed the practice of Brahman at the conclusion of the treatise.
For those intent upon that [liberation], disregard for the duties previously mentioned by oneself has been stated;
this very Śruti is the source of such Smṛti.
Everything has the form of Śāmbavī.

For there is no difference in the contemplation (*bhāvana*) of Tripurasundarī whether one performs what is prescribed or what is prohibited. The sense is that bondage arises from the performance of injunctions and prohibitions only for those who have fallen away due to a lack of such contemplation. Therefore:
The words of the Blessed One.
"If there should be a lapse in the ritual duties of men performing my rites, thirty million great sages perform those rites for them. Thus [it is said].
The traditional scriptures do not exist.

Because it is already known, even the Vedas do not apply with respect to it. For this very reason, the venerable teacher [Śaṅkara] stated in the *Adhyāsa-bhāṣya*: "The scriptures have as their object those who possess ignorance. This was said in the two sūtras concerning the two types of permission (*abhyanujñā*), which take the form of explanatory statements (*arthavāda*) providing reasons.
The Guru is one.

This goal is attained through devotion to a single Guru characterized by the aforementioned qualifications; for if there were a multiplicity of Gurus, there would be a discrepancy in their instructions.
Because doubt is inevitable; for this very reason, it is stated in the Paraśurāmakalpasūtra:
"The worship of a single guru is free from doubt."
"Having properly obtained a family preceptor, one should not resort to another teacher. Thus it is said.

This scriptural statement is the source for the prohibition mentioned in the *Kulārṇava*. By the very use of the word "having obtained," the statement from the *Śaktirahasya*— that "there are infinite gurus in the Kaula tradition"—
is intended to refer to the case where such a guru is not found.
Those who possess the cognition of the unity of all things.

The suffix *ṣyañ* is used here in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*). Proceeding in this manner, even a practitioner (*sādhaka*) attains nothing but the realization of non-duality (*advaita-buddhi*) at the time of death.
Because of the accomplishment through the mantra.
This is the heading. The meaning is that from this point onward, those rules (*niyama*) which are to be observed prior to the attainment of mantra-siddhi are being described as *dharmas*.
Therefore, the implication is that if even one of the rules to be mentioned hereafter is disregarded, there will surely be a loss of accomplishment (*siddhi*).
Intoxication and the like should be abandoned.
Intoxication (*mada*) is a specific disorder produced by the consumption of the ingredients of a *modaka* (sweetmeat).
The group of six internal enemies (ariṣaḍvarga), which are to be grasped by terms such as "modification" (vikāra) and "end" (anta), must indeed be abandoned.
However, after the attainment of success in mantra (mantrasiddhi), desire, anger, and the like do not manifest of their own accord;
yet, specific modifications have already been permitted previously. And so it is said:
As long as the gaze does not waver, one should drink the substance down to the throat;

since there is no contradiction between these two statements because they are established as referring respectively to the practitioner of mantra (*mantrasādhaka*) and the one who has mastered the mantra (*siddhamantra*).
One should not make it manifest.

Those who lack initiation into and worship of their own mantra, who are excessively devoted to other religious systems, and who are mere semblances of practitioners of their own mantra— all such people are "outward-facing" (bahirmukha);
one should conceal one's practice in such a way that they do not recognize, "This person is a practitioner of this [mantra]."

And this is the same even in other initiations (*dīkṣā*), because of such statements found in their respective contexts as: "Those who are uninitiated do not look upon him while he is observing his vow," and so forth.

Although its secrecy is established simply because it is prescribed in the *Āraṇyakakāṇḍa* of the Vedas— just like the *Pravargya* rite which is an auxiliary of a sacrifice (*kratvaṅga*)— nevertheless, its prescription is stated once again in explicit words to distinguish it from other secret teachings.

This is for the sake of distinguishing it [from other teachings]. While in other doctrines a breach of secrecy results merely in a deficiency of the ritual (*kratuviguṇya*), here, if that occurs, there is indeed hell. Thus says the Lord Paraśurāma: "From its manifestation comes hell."
One should not engage in conversation with animals.

"All those who are outward-turned are indeed bound souls (paśu) because they are devoid of knowledge; for this [Vedic] knowledge alone is true knowledge. The term 'learned' (vidvat) is not applied to one endowed with knowledge of crafts and the like," according to such statements. Together with them, [one should practice] correctly...
One should not speak until one's own heart has been made known;
therefore, there is no prohibition against speaking on the surface.
Injustice is justice.
Even if some talkative person should disparage the Kaulika practice by means of the principles of the Purva and Uttara Mīmāṃsā, one should not feel even the slightest anger;
with this intention, he says: "anyāya," where the negative particle (nañ) has the sense of "little," meaning a weak argument.

This means "the logic of the prima facie position" (*pūrvapakṣanyāya*). That too is indeed a form of reasoning (*nyāya*); for even the prima facie position does not proceed without the presentation of reasoning.
Therefore, this path, though established by such reasoning, is itself entirely logical (*nyāyya*). And it is not thus...
Since there are exceptions according to the logic of established tenets (*siddhāntanyāya*), how can there be confidence in those tenets?

For they are manifold due to the differences among the sages, and their proponents establish them in various ways that are mutually contradictory, occurring within both the earlier and later systems (*tantra*).

Because it is seen many times in such [sections] as the Devatādhikaraṇa, the sense is that the weakness lies with the disputant, not with the reasoning. Thus says the venerable Vyāsa: "On account of the instability of reasoning."
"Indeed, those entities which are inconceivable should not be joined with ratiocination. Thus it is said.
For it is appropriate to present such principles— which have the singular fruit of mental concentration— only in a manner that does not contradict the tradition; just as,
even though each subsequent one among the Śruti, Smṛti, and tradition is weaker than the preceding one.
In the present tantra, the opposite should be inferred. Nor is this an extreme impropriety,
for even those learned in the Dharmaśāstras have frequently accepted the restriction of each preceding stage by each succeeding one.
One should not count anyone at all.
One should not even count Brahmā as one who speaks in contradiction to his own established doctrine;
the meaning is that one should place absolute trust [in him]. For this very reason, there is the traditional rule (*kalpa*) that authority consists primarily in trustworthiness.
One should not speak of one's own secrets.
The meaning is that one should not speak even to a friend for fear of the disclosure [of the secret].
He should speak to the disciple.

Therefore, the Smṛti states: "It has reached the surface of the earth through oral instruction from ear to ear. Since such matters are to be known solely through this kind of tradition, in regard to subjects of this nature, the conduct of the virtuous (sadācāra) is indeed more authoritative than Śruti and Smṛti.
One should infer accordingly that, from the perspective of its grammatical derivation, it is like the practice of correct application (*satprayoga*), and so forth.
Internally Śākta, externally Śaiva, and in the world Vaiṣṇava.
Even though it is not manifest, he clarifies that it must indeed be performed: "The worship of the Power, which is to be known solely by the internal organ, must be practiced."
For those who follow the Śākta tradition, a drop of red sandalwood paste is desired between the eyebrows.
Thus, even though these signs are recognized,
they must be performed while being concealed by Śaiva marks such as the wearing of sacred ashes (vibhūti) and so forth.

Because even Śiva is non-different from Śakti; for through such statements as "I alone am the masculine form, the nectar for the eyes of the Gopīs," the essential nature of Viṣṇu is shown to be identical with the inner self of Tripurasundarī, who is the manifest form of Paraśiva’s consort.
The meaning of these three aphorisms is that one should manifest the very worship of Viṣṇu in assemblies by means of the repeated chanting of Viṣṇu’s names and so forth. For this very reason,
there is an increase in the excellence of the fruits for Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Śakti respectively.
It is stated in the *Rahasyanāmasāhasra* with the intention of [revealing] ever-higher secrets:
This indeed is the proper conduct.

There are other practices of the Kaulikas prescribed in the Tantras as well; among all of them, the meaning is that the practice consisting in the absence of manifesting [one's identity] is by far the most principal.

In this context, it is stated for the purpose of illuminating that liberation comes from the knowledge of the Self, and that while one should indeed be intensely devoted to right conduct as in the case of ritual action, one must not be negligent in the inquiry into the Self; rather, one should properly practice both.
Again, the reminder.
All the various philosophical systems (darśanas), which have flowed through the world in an unbroken stream from time immemorial and are free from reproach,
are indeed authoritative for their respective qualified practitioners; they are so in every respect.

One should not criticize it; for by criticizing it, doubt arises among those who are its rightful practitioners, leading to a lack of confidence even in the philosophical system one has adopted oneself.
Furthermore, due to the loss of eligibility even for the Kaula tradition, one falls from both paths and perishes like a scattered cloud.
Because of the risk of incurring a curse, there would be a defect resulting in the lay follower (*upāsaka*) becoming subject to censure;
for this very reason, Lord Kṛṣṇa said: "One should not cause confusion of mind in the ignorant who are attached to action," and Bhagavān Rāma stated: "Non-censuring of all philosophical systems."
Thus with respect to the internal.
In response to the doubt as to what purpose is served by not censuring any philosophical system (*sarvadarśana*), he says:

since others face destruction like a scattered cloud, and because one’s own state of being the Self of all would otherwise suffer a deficiency, this conduct also serves only those who possess self-knowledge (*ātmajña*). This is the meaning.
One should not perform a vow.

One should not perform those vows that take the form of human goals (*puruṣārtha*), because there is no goal to be attained through them that exceeds even this [liberation]. As for those which take the form of the duties of caste and stage of life (*varṇāśramadharma*) and are obtained as means for accomplishing human goals—

The observances (*vratas*) pertaining to the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), which are established as ancillaries (*aṅga*) to the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites such as the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), must indeed be performed;
for there is no injunction for their abandonment in the case of obligatory and occasional rites.
One should not remain fixed by rule.
This is its explanation: because restriction, being of the nature of compulsion, is opposed to the contemplation of the Self.
From [the practice of] restrictive observances, there is no liberation.
The meaning is that liberation would be delayed precisely because of the absence of inquiry into the Self.
One should not perform the Kaula consecration.

If someone skilled in presenting logical arguments were able to establish the Kaula system through those very arguments, even he would not establish this path, for fear of violating its requirement of secrecy. Therefore...

Thus, regarding this subject matter of the scripture, since even for the author it constitutes the establishment of the Kaula tradition, and because there is the application of prohibitions therein as well, certain traditional portions must be understood from the mouth of the Guru alone, so that they remain unmanifest.
In each respective case, the written record accords.
One should be equal toward all.

Extracting this very principle from the scriptures through established practice, it prescribes: "One should be equal toward every living being, whether mobile or immobile; one should conduct oneself with single-minded devotion. For this very reason, the *Bhāgavata* states: "The ether, wind, fire, water, and earth," and so forth.
He who is fully liberated is liberated immediately from such a preeminent person; however,
those who are slightly inferior are nevertheless gradually liberated— this is the intended meaning.
Having risen at dawn, the teacher should recite these sūtras;
for him, the attainment of the Command shall occur—such is the command of the Supreme Lord.

Now, he who recites these sūtras preceded by such a continuous connection (anusandhāna) is indeed the teacher; for him alone there is the accomplishment of the Command (ājñāsiddhi), which is to say, unimpeded authority and the state of Śiva. Thus, this is the Command of the Supreme Lord; therefore, one should not entertain any lack of confidence.
Such is the intended meaning.
Even one who is devoid of proper conduct, or one who does not perform worship,
if he respects his elder, rejoices in the Nandana grove.
He who does not practice the conduct previously described, and whose mind is clouded by doubt, does not perform the worship according to the prescribed method;
the transposition of words is a Vedic (chāndasa) usage. He does not [believe] that "this path is the most excellent of all."

He thinks thus: "Even such a mere semblance of a worshipper (upāsakābhāsa) certainly attains at least heaven, despite not obtaining the aforementioned fruit; how much more so, then, for one who worships correctly, that he should obtain the fruit as described. Thus [ends the section].
The Commentary on the Kaulopaniṣad, composed by the illustrious Bhāskararāya, who has reached the further shore of the ocean of the Kaula path, is complete.
Thus. May there be prosperity.
